0001: \section{Fibonacci prime-power realization}
0002: \label{sec:prime-power-realization}
0003: 
0004: The witness-cover classification is structural.  We now supply the
0005: Fibonacci-specific input that determines which prime powers can occur in its
0006: rank-jump families.  These formulas will be used explicitly in the upper bounds.
0007: 
0008: \begin{proposition}[Classical prime-power rank lifting]
0009: \label{prop:prime-power-ladders}
0010: Let $p$ be prime, and put $z_p:=\alpha(p)$. For $p\ne2,5$, put
0011: $h_p:=\nu_p(F_{z_p})$. Then
0012: \[
0013: \alpha(2)=3,\qquad \alpha(4)=6,\qquad
0014: \alpha(2^e)=3\cdot2^{e-2}\quad(e\ge3),
0015: \]
0016: \[
0017: \alpha(5^e)=5^e\quad(e\ge1),
0018: \]
0019: and, for $p\ne2,5$,
0020: \[
0021: \alpha(p^e)=p^{\max\{e-h_p,0\}}z_p\quad(e\ge1).
0022: \]
0023: \end{proposition}
0024: 
0025: \begin{proof}
0026: Wall's rank-divisibility theorem gives
0027: \[
0028: p\mid F_r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z_p\mid r
0029: \]
0030: \cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm}. For $p\ne2,5$, the classical congruence
0031: \[
0032: F_{p-(5/p)}\equiv0\pmod p
0033: \]
0034: gives $z_p\mid p-(5/p)$, so $p\nmid z_p$. Lengyel's valuation formula
0035: \cite[Theorems~1 and~2]{Lengyel1995OrderFibonacciLucas}, in the treatment of
0036: Medina--Rowland \cite{MedinaRowland2015PRegularity}, states that when
0037: $z_p\mid r$,
0038: \[
0039: \nu_p(F_r)=\nu_p(F_{z_p})+\nu_p(r).
0040: \]
0041: Writing $r=z_pu$ yields
0042: $\nu_p(F_{z_pu})=h_p+\nu_p(u)$. Thus $p^e\mid F_{z_pu}$ if and only if
0043: $\nu_p(u)\ge e-h_p$, and the least admissible $u$ is
0044: $p^{\max\{e-h_p,0\}}$.
0045: 
0046: For the exceptional primes, the same valuation formulas specialize to
0047: \[
0048: \nu_5(F_r)=\nu_5(r),
0049: \qquad
0050: \nu_2(F_r)=
0051: \begin{cases}
0052: 0, & 3\nmid r,\\
0053: 1, & r\equiv3\pmod 6,\\
0054: 3, & r\equiv6\pmod {12},\\
0055: \nu_2(r)+2, & 12\mid r.
0056: \end{cases}
0057: \]
0058: The least index divisible by $5^e$ is $5^e$. For $2$, the least indices
0059: with valuation at least $1$, $2$, and $3$ are $3$, $6$, and $6$; for
0060: $e\ge4$ the least admissible multiple of $12$ is $3\cdot2^{e-2}$.
0061: \end{proof}
0062: 
0063: \begin{corollary}[Rank-jump prime-power classification]
0064: \label{cor:rank-jump-classification}
0065: The rank-jump prime powers are exactly the following:
0066: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
0067: \item $2\in\Atom(3)$, $4\in\Atom(6)$, and
0068: $2^e\in\Atom(3\cdot2^{e-2})$ for every $e\ge4$; the power $8$ is not
0069: rank-jump.
0070: \item $5^e\in\Atom(5^e)$ for every $e\ge1$.
0071: \item If $p\ne2,5$, $z_p=\alpha(p)$, and
0072: $h_p=\nu_p(F_{z_p})$, then $p\in\Atom(z_p)$ and
0073: $p^e\in\Atom(p^{e-h_p}z_p)$ for every $e>h_p$; no power $p^e$ with
0074: $1<e\le h_p$ is rank-jump.
0075: \end{enumerate}
0076: Consequently every rank-jump factor is either a prime jump or a ladder jump $p^e$ with
0077: $e>1$. Every ladder step changes only the $p$-adic coordinate of its
0078: apparition index when it is lowered to $p^{e-1}$.
0079: \end{corollary}
0080: 
0081: \begin{proof}
0082: Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders}. For $p=2$, the ranks are
0083: $3,6,6,12,24,\ldots$ on $2,4,8,16,32,\ldots$. For $p=5$, every step is
0084: rank-jump. If $p\ne2,5$, the rank remains $z_p$ for $1\le e\le h_p$ and then
0085: gains one factor of $p$ at each further level. The last assertion follows
0086: from the same formulas.
0087: \end{proof}
0088: 
0089: \begin{lemma}[Prime-ladder dichotomy]
0090: \label{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}
0091: Let $\theta=p^e\in\Atom(d)$ and suppose $d\mid n$. If $e=1$, then
0092: \[
0093: E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta).
0094: \]
0095: If $e>1$, then $E_n(\theta)$ is either empty or the singleton $\{p\}$.
0096: In particular, no Fibonacci rank-jump factor has
0097: \[
0098: 1<\#E_n(\theta)<\#T_n(\theta).
0099: \]
0100: \end{lemma}
0101: 
0102: \begin{proof}
0103: If $e=1$, then $d^-(\theta)=\alpha(1)=1$, so every coordinate in
0104: $T_n(\theta)$ is lost after lowering. Assume $e>1$. By
0105: Corollary~\ref{cor:rank-jump-classification}, $\theta$ is a ladder jump.
0106: Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders} shows that $d(\theta)$ and
0107: $d^-(\theta)$ differ only in their $p$-adic coordinate. Therefore the only
0108: full coordinate that can be lost is $p$ itself, and the result follows.
0109: \end{proof}
0110: 
0111: For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, define the prime window
0112: \[
0113: P_J(n):=\coprod_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)=J}}\Pi_\alpha(d),
0114: \]
0115: where $T_n(d)=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):
0116: \nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}$.  A prime in $P_J(n)$ is identified with its
0117: prime jump.
0118: 
0119: \begin{proposition}[Rank-jump families and unique ladder slots]
0120: \label{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots}
0121: Let $n\ge3$ and let $\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$.
0122: Then every rank-jump factor in $\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)$ is either in the prime window
0123: $P_J(n)$, which occurs only when $I=J$, or in a ladder family with
0124: $I=\{p\}$ for a prime coordinate $p\in J$.  Each such ladder family contains
0125: at most one rank-jump factor.
0126: 
0127: More precisely, put $a=\nu_p(n)$.  Its only possible ladder jump is
0128: \[
0129: \lambda_p(n)=
0130: \begin{cases}
0131: 4, & p=2,\ a=1,\\
0132: 2^{a+2}, & p=2,\ a\ge2,\\
0133: 5^a, & p=5,\ a\ge2,\\
0134: p^{h_p+a}, & p\notin\{2,5\},
0135: \end{cases}
0136: \]
0137: with no candidate for $p=5$, $a=1$.  The candidate belongs to
0138: $\mathcal A_{\{p\},J}(n)$ exactly when
0139: $d(\lambda_p(n))\mid n$ and $T_n(\lambda_p(n))=J$.
0140: Consequently every rank-jump family is finite, every nonsingleton rank-jump family
0141: is a finite disjoint union of exact-rank prime classes, and every labelled
0142: ladder slot has at most one candidate.
0143: \end{proposition}
0144: 
0145: \begin{proof}
0146: If $\theta=q$ is a prime jump, the prime-ladder dichotomy gives
0147: $E_n(q)=T_n(q)$, and $q$ belongs to the unique class
0148: $\Pi_\alpha(d(q))$ in $P_{T_n(q)}(n)$. Conversely every prime in $P_J(n)$
0149: has $(E_n,T_n)=(J,J)$.
0150: 
0151: Suppose $\theta=q^e$ is a ladder jump. The same dichotomy gives
0152: $E_n(\theta)=\{q\}$ whenever the essential support is nonempty. Hence its
0153: essential coordinate determines its underlying prime, so $q=p$. The
0154: full-exponent equation
0155: $\nu_p(d(p^e))=\nu_p(n)=a$ and
0156: Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders} now leave only the displayed
0157: candidate. For $p=2$, the rank-jump ladder levels are $4$ of rank $6$ and
0158: $2^e$ of rank $3\cdot2^{e-2}$ for $e\ge4$. For $p=5$, the rank is $5^e$,
0159: and $e=1$ is a prime jump. For $p\notin\{2,5\}$, one has
0160: $p\nmid z_p$ and
0161: $\alpha(p^e)=p^{e-h_p}z_p$ at rank-jump ladder levels, so $e=h_p+a$.
0162: The remaining conditions $d(\theta)\mid n$ and $T_n(\theta)=J$ are exactly
0163: the conditions for membership in $\mathcal A_{\{p\},J}(n)$.
0164: 
0165: Finally, each $\Pi_\alpha(d)$ is finite by
0166: Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}, and there are only finitely many
0167: divisors $d$ of $n$. This proves all finiteness and uniqueness assertions.
0168: \end{proof}

0001: \section{Rank level sets and witness covers}\label{sec:upper-fibers}
0002: %% ====================================================================
0003: 
0004: The first two lemmas in this section use only rank divisibility and the lcm
0005: identity. They are included to fix the structural framework and are not
0006: presented as new Fibonacci identities. The witness-cover theorem packages
0007: their minimality conditions for the subsequent Fibonacci analysis.
0008: The underlying deletion-one-factor condition is classical: Wagner called
0009: divisor tuples satisfying it minimal multiplicative covers of an integer
0010: \cite{Wagner1978MultiplicativeCovers}, as a multiplicative generalization of
0011: the minimal set covers studied by Hearne--Wagner
0012: \cite{HearneWagner1973MinimalCovers}. Proposition~
0013: \ref{prop:wagner-comparison} states the exact boundary between that skeleton
0014: and the lowered-label structure used here.
0015: 
0016: The notation $B_n$ below is local. As a mathematical object it is simply the
0017: level set $\alpha^{-1}(n)$, and passing to $\mathcal M_n$ is the generic
0018: operation of taking minimal elements in a finite poset.
0019: 
0020: \begin{definition}\label{def:birth-layer}
0021: For $n\ge2$ let
0022: \[
0023: D_n:=\operatorname{Div}(F_n),\qquad
0024: B_n:=\{q\in D_n:\ \alpha(q)=n\},\qquad
0025: A(n):=\#B_n.
0026: \]
0027: The set $B_n$ is partially ordered by divisibility. Its set of minimal
0028: elements is
0029: \[
0030: \mathcal M_n:=\{m\in B_n:\ \text{there is no }q\in B_n
0031: \text{ with }q\mid m\text{ and }q<m\},
0032: \]
0033: and
0034: \[
0035: \widthop(B_n):=\max\{\#\mathcal A:\ \mathcal A\subseteq B_n
0036: \text{ is an antichain}\}.
0037: \]
0038: We write $\mathcal P(n)$ for the set of prime divisors of $n$. Since
0039: $F_2=1$, we use the boundary convention
0040: \[
0041: B_2=\mathcal M_2=\varnothing,\qquad A(2)=\widthop(B_2)=0.
0042: \]
0043: \end{definition}
0044: 
0045: \begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
0046: For every $n\ge2$,
0047: \[
0048: B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.
0049: \]
0050: Moreover $B_n$ is an upper set in $D_n$: if $q\in B_n$, $r\in D_n$, and
0051: $q\mid r$, then $r\in B_n$. Consequently
0052: \[
0053: B_n=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M_n}\{q\in D_n:\ m\mid q\}.
0054: \]
0055: \end{lemma}
0056: 
0057: \begin{proof}
0058: By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}, an integer $q$ lies in $D_m$ if and
0059: only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$. Thus $q\in D_n$ lies outside
0060: $\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}$ precisely when $\alpha(q)\mid n$ but
0061: $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every prime $p\mid n$.
0062: 
0063: If $\alpha(q)=n$, then clearly $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every $p\mid n$, so
0064: $q$ is outside the union. Conversely, suppose $\alpha(q)\mid n$ and
0065: $\alpha(q)<n$. Then $n/\alpha(q)>1$; choose a prime $p$ dividing
0066: $n/\alpha(q)$. Since $\alpha(q)\mid n/p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}
0067: gives $q\in D_{n/p}$, contrary to being outside the union. Hence the
0068: complement is exactly the set of $q\in D_n$ with $\alpha(q)=n$, namely
0069: $B_n$. For $n=2$ this also gives
0070: $B_2=D_2\setminus D_1=\varnothing$ under the boundary convention in
0071: Definition~\ref{def:birth-layer}.
0072: 
0073: Now let $q\in B_n$, $r\in D_n$, and $q\mid r$. Since $r\in D_n$,
0074: $\alpha(r)\mid n$. Since $q\mid r$, every Fibonacci number divisible by $r$
0075: is divisible by $q$; applying the divisibility criterion to
0076: $F_{\alpha(r)}$ gives $\alpha(q)\mid\alpha(r)$. But $\alpha(q)=n$, so
0077: $n\mid\alpha(r)$ and $\alpha(r)\mid n$, whence $\alpha(r)=n$. Therefore
0078: $r\in B_n$.
0079: 
0080: Finally $D_n$ is finite, so every element $q\in B_n$ has at least one
0081: minimal element $m$ of $B_n$ below it in the divisibility order. The upper-set
0082: property gives the reverse containment: every element of $D_n$ divisible by
0083: some $m\in\mathcal M_n$ lies again in $B_n$. This proves the displayed
0084: decomposition.
0085: \end{proof}
0086: 
0087: \begin{lemma}[Minimal-lcm criterion]\label{thm:minimal-generators}
0088: Let $n\ge2$, and let
0089: $m=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ be a divisor of $F_n$, with the $p_i$ distinct
0090: and $e_i\ge1$. Put
0091: \[
0092: \lambda_i:=\alpha(p_i^{e_i}),\qquad
0093: \lambda_i^-:=\alpha(p_i^{e_i-1}),
0094: \]
0095: where $\alpha(1)=1$. Then $m\in\mathcal M_n$ if and only if
0096: \begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm-criterion}
0097: \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)=n
0098: \quad\text{and}\quad
0099: \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,
0100: \lambda_{i+1},\ldots,\lambda_r)<n
0101: \quad(1\le i\le r).
0102: \end{equation}
0103: \end{lemma}
0104: 
0105: \begin{proof}
0106: Because $m\mid F_n$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives
0107: $\lambda_i\mid n$ for every $i$. Applying the lcm identity in
0108: Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} repeatedly gives
0109: \[
0110: \alpha(m)=\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r).
0111: \]
0112: Thus the first condition in \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion} is equivalent to
0113: $m\in B_n$.
0114: 
0115: Assume first that $m\in\mathcal M_n$. Then $m\in B_n$, so the first lcm is
0116: $n$. For a fixed $i$, the integer $m/p_i$ is a proper divisor of $m$ and is
0117: still a divisor of $F_n$. Minimality of $m$ in $B_n$ implies
0118: $m/p_i\notin B_n$. Since $\alpha(m/p_i)\mid n$, this is equivalent to
0119: $\alpha(m/p_i)<n$. A second application of the lcm identity gives
0120: \[
0121: \alpha(m/p_i)=
0122: \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,
0123: \lambda_{i+1},\ldots,\lambda_r),
0124: \]
0125: which is the lowered prime-power condition in
0126: \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion}.
0127: 
0128: Conversely, suppose \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion} holds. The first condition gives
0129: $m\in B_n$. Let $q$ be any proper divisor of $m$. Then for at least one
0130: index $i$ the exponent of $p_i$ in $q$ is at most $e_i-1$. Hence
0131: \[
0132: \alpha(q)\mid
0133: \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,
0134: \lambda_{i+1},\ldots,\lambda_r),
0135: \]
0136: again by the lcm identity and by monotonicity under divisibility of prime
0137: powers. The right-hand side is $<n$ by
0138: \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion}. Since $q\mid m\mid F_n$, we also have
0139: $\alpha(q)\mid n$, and therefore $\alpha(q)<n$. Thus no proper divisor of
0140: $m$ lies in $B_n$, so $m$ is minimal in $B_n$.
0141: \end{proof}
0142: 
0143: \subsection*{Witness covers}
0144: 
0145: \begin{definition}\label{def:witness-cover}
0146: An \emph{$n$-witness cover} is a finite set
0147: $\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ of rank-jump prime powers satisfying:
0148: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
0149: \item $d(\theta)\mid n$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$;
0150: \item the elements of $\Theta$ are pairwise coprime;
0151: \item the full-coordinate supports cover all prime coordinates of $n$,
0152: \[
0153: \bigcup_{\theta\in\Theta}T_n(\theta)=\mathcal P(n);
0154: \]
0155: \item each rank-jump factor has an essential coordinate not supplied by the other rank-jump factors,
0156: \[
0157: E_n(\theta)\nsubseteq
0158: \bigcup_{\eta\in\Theta,\ \eta\ne\theta}T_n(\eta)
0159: \qquad(\theta\in\Theta).
0160: \]
0161: \end{enumerate}
0162: The last condition is the irredundance condition. It is stated with
0163: $E_n$ rather than $T_n$ because overlapping full-coordinate support is
0164: allowed; what is forbidden is that every coordinate lost by lowering
0165: $\theta$ is already supplied at full exponent by the remaining rank-jump factors.
0166: \end{definition}
0167: 
0168: \begin{lemma}[Coordinate test for lowering one rank-jump factor]
0169: \label{lem:coordinate-lowering-test}
0170: Let $n\ge2$, and let
0171: $\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ be a pairwise coprime set of rank-jump
0172: prime powers with $d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and
0173: \[
0174: \lcmop(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r))=n.
0175: \]
0176: Fix $\theta_i=p_i^{e_i}$, and put
0177: \[
0178: N_i^-:=\lcmop\bigl(d^-(\theta_i),\ d(\theta_j):j\ne i\bigr).
0179: \]
0180: Then $N_i^-=n$ if and only if
0181: \[
0182: E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j).
0183: \]
0184: Equivalently, lowering $\theta_i$ to $p_i^{e_i-1}$ keeps the apparition lcm
0185: equal to $n$ exactly when every coordinate lost by the lowering is supplied at
0186: full exponent by some other rank-jump factor. If
0187: $\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, then
0188: $\nu_\ell(N_i^-)<\nu_\ell(n)$, so $N_i^-<n$.
0189: \end{lemma}
0190: 
0191: \begin{proof}
0192: Since $d^-(\theta_i)\mid d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and $d(\theta_j)\mid n$ for
0193: $j\ne i$, the integer $N_i^-$ divides $n$. Hence $N_i^-=n$ is equivalent to
0194: saying that every prime coordinate $\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$ occurs in $N_i^-$
0195: with valuation $\nu_\ell(n)$.
0196: 
0197: Assume first that
0198: $E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, and fix
0199: $\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$. Because the original lcm is $n$, at least one of the
0200: numbers $d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r)$ supplies the full
0201: $\ell$-adic valuation of $n$. If such a supplier is some $d(\theta_j)$ with
0202: $j\ne i$, then $\ell\in T_n(\theta_j)$ and the same full valuation appears in
0203: $N_i^-$. The only remaining case is that $\theta_i$ itself supplies the full
0204: valuation and no other rank-jump factor does, so $\ell\in T_n(\theta_i)$ and
0205: $\ell\notin\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The assumed containment then gives
0206: $\ell\notin E_n(\theta_i)$. By the definition of $E_n(\theta_i)$,
0207: $\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))=\nu_\ell(n)$, so the lowered factor still supplies the
0208: full $\ell$-coordinate in $N_i^-$. Thus every coordinate of $n$ is still
0209: present at full valuation, and $N_i^-=n$.
0210: 
0211: Conversely, suppose that some coordinate
0212: $\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ is not in $\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The
0213: membership $\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ says
0214: $\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))<\nu_\ell(n)$. For every $j\ne i$, the exclusion
0215: $\ell\notin T_n(\theta_j)$ says
0216: $\nu_\ell(d(\theta_j))<\nu_\ell(n)$. Therefore the lcm defining $N_i^-$ also
0217: has $\ell$-adic valuation strictly below $\nu_\ell(n)$. Since $N_i^-\mid n$,
0218: this proves $N_i^-<n$.
0219: \end{proof}
0220: 
0221: \begin{proposition}[Wagner comparison and lowered labels]
0222: \label{prop:wagner-comparison}
0223: Let $n\ge2$, and let $\Theta=\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$ be a set of distinct prime
0224: rank-jump factors with $d_i:=\alpha(p_i)\mid n$. Then $\Theta$ is an $n$-witness cover
0225: if and only if, after forgetting the order of the tuple
0226: $(d_1,\ldots,d_r)$,
0227: \begin{equation}\label{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover}
0228:  \lcmop(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=n,
0229:  \qquad
0230:  \lcmop(d_1,\ldots,\widehat{d_i},\ldots,d_r)<n
0231:  \quad(1\le i\le r).
0232: \end{equation}
0233: Thus the prime-jump case is precisely the unordered form of Wagner's minimal
0234: multiplicative cover condition.
0235: 
0236: For arbitrary pairwise coprime jumps
0237: $\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$, the witness condition replaces the
0238: deletion in \eqref{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover} by
0239: \begin{equation}\label{eq:lowered-label-multiplicative-cover}
0240:  \lcmop\bigl(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d^-(\theta_i),\ldots,
0241:  d(\theta_r)\bigr)<n
0242:  \quad(1\le i\le r).
0243: \end{equation}
0244: In particular, ladder jumps supply the predecessor-decorated case: their
0245: label is lowered to $d^-(\theta_i)$ rather than deleted.
0246: \end{proposition}
0247: 
0248: \begin{proof}
0249: For a prime jump $p_i$, one has $d^-(p_i)=\alpha(1)=1$. Hence replacing
0250: $d_i$ by $d^-(p_i)$ in an lcm is identical to omitting $d_i$. Lemma~
0251: \ref{thm:minimal-generators} and Lemma~\ref{lem:coordinate-lowering-test}
0252: then identify the witness-cover conditions with
0253: \eqref{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover}. Since the labels form a
0254: minimal cover, no repeated label can occur; forgetting tuple order therefore
0255: produces the corresponding unordered cover without a multiplicity ambiguity.
0256: 
0257: For arbitrary rank-jump factors, the same two lemmas say exactly that the full apparition
0258: lcm is $n$ and that lowering each rank-jump factor produces
0259: \eqref{eq:lowered-label-multiplicative-cover}. The final assertion is the
0260: distinction between $d^-(p)=1$ for prime jumps and the nontrivial lower rank
0261: of a ladder jump.
0262: \end{proof}
0263: 
0264: Wagner's condition and its set-theoretic predecessor supply the classical
0265: cover skeleton. The Fibonacci-specific content below is the arithmetic
0266: realization of its labels by exact-rank primes, the predecessor-lowering
0267: admissibility test forced by prime-power ladders, and the correspondence with
0268: $\mathcal M_n$. The canonical squarefree slice and its exact weighted count
0269: in Section~\ref{sec:rank-pure} are further arithmetic consequences of that
0270: realization.
0271: 
0272: \begin{theorem}\label{thm:witness-classification}
0273: For every $n\ge 2$, multiplication gives a bijection
0274: \[
0275: \Theta\longmapsto \prod_{\theta\in\Theta}\theta
0276: \]
0277: from the set of $n$-witness covers onto $\mathcal M_n$. Its inverse sends
0278: $m\in\mathcal M_n$ to the set
0279: \[
0280: \Theta(m):=\{p^{\nu_p(m)}:p\mid m\}
0281: \]
0282: of prime-power factors occurring in the prime factorization of $m$. In
0283: particular,
0284: \[
0285: \mathcal M_n=\bigl\{\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}\theta:
0286: \Theta\text{ is an $n$-witness cover}\bigr\},
0287: \]
0288: and each element of $\mathcal M_n$ has a unique witness-cover factorization.
0289: Here uniqueness is inherited from unique factorization in $\mathbb Z$; the
0290: substantive assertion is the witness-cover admissibility criterion.
0291: \end{theorem}
0292: 
0293: \begin{proof}
0294: Let $m\in\mathcal M_n$, and write its prime factorization as
0295: $m=\prod_{i=1}^r\theta_i$ with $\theta_i=p_i^{e_i}$ and the $p_i$ distinct.
0296: Each $\theta_i$ is rank-jump: if $\alpha(p_i^{e_i-1})=\alpha(p_i^{e_i})$, then
0297: replacing $\theta_i$ by $p_i^{e_i-1}$ preserves the lcm, contradicting
0298: the minimal-generator criterion in
0299: Lemma~\ref{thm:minimal-generators}. Since
0300: $n=\lcmop(d(\theta_i))$, the sets $T_n(\theta_i)$ cover $\mathcal P(n)$. The
0301: condition $\alpha(m/p_i)<n$ forces
0302: $E_n(\theta_i)\nsubseteq\bigcup_{j\neq i}T_n(\theta_j)$; otherwise the lost
0303: coordinates would be supplied by other factors, keeping the lcm equal to $n$.
0304: Thus $\{\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r\}$ is an $n$-witness cover.
0305: 
0306: Conversely, let $\Theta$ be an $n$-witness cover and
0307: $m=\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}\theta$. By
0308: the lcm property recorded in Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics},
0309: $\alpha(m)=\lcmop(d(\theta):\theta\in\Theta)=n$. For each
0310: $\theta=p^e\in\Theta$, the witness condition
0311: provides $\ell\in E_n(\theta)\setminus\bigcup_{\eta\neq\theta}T_n(\eta)$; at
0312: this coordinate, $\alpha(m/p)<n$.
0313: Lemma~\ref{thm:minimal-generators} then gives $m\in\mathcal M_n$.
0314: 
0315: It remains to record injectivity and the stated inverse.  If two witness covers
0316: $\Theta$ and $\Theta'$ have the same product, then unique factorization in
0317: $\mathbb Z$ gives the same underlying primes with the same exponents in the two
0318: products.  Since the elements of each witness cover are pairwise coprime prime
0319: powers, those prime-power factors are exactly the elements of the cover.  Hence
0320: $\Theta=\Theta'$.  Therefore multiplication is injective, while the first
0321: paragraph shows that the prime-power factor set $\Theta(m)$ of every
0322: $m\in\mathcal M_n$ is an $n$-witness cover and the second paragraph shows that
0323: every $n$-witness cover maps into $\mathcal M_n$.  Thus multiplication is the
0324: claimed bijection, with inverse $m\mapsto\Theta(m)$.
0325: \end{proof}
0326: 
0327: \begin{corollary}\label{cor:support-bound}
0328: Every $m\in\mathcal M_n$ satisfies $\omega(m)\le\omega(n)$.
0329: \end{corollary}
0330: 
0331: \begin{proof}
0332: The witness condition provides an injection
0333: $\theta\mapsto\ell(\theta)$ from $\Theta$ into $\mathcal P(n)$: choose
0334: $\ell(\theta)\in E_n(\theta)\setminus\bigcup_{\eta\neq\theta}T_n(\eta)$.
0335: Hence $\omega(m)=\#\Theta\le\omega(n)$.
0336: \end{proof}

0001: \section{Rank-pure covers and the canonical squarefree slice}
0002: \label{sec:rank-pure}
0003: 
0004: For a finite set $V$, write $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ for the set of
0005: irredundant covers of $V$ by distinct nonempty subsets: a family
0006: $\mathcal C$ belongs to $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ when
0007: $\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal C}S=V$ and every $S\in\mathcal C$ contains an element
0008: outside $\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal C\setminus\{S\}}T$.
0009: 
0010: \begin{theorem}[Rank-pure universality]\label{thm:rank-pure-universality}
0011: Let $n\ge3$, put $V=\mathcal P(n)$, and, for every nonempty $S\subseteq V$,
0012: define
0013: \[
0014:  n_S:=\prod_{\ell\in S}\ell^{\nu_\ell(n)},\qquad
0015:  a_n(S):=\#\Pi_\alpha(n_S),
0016: \]
0017: and
0018: \[
0019:  \mathcal E_n:=\{S\subseteq V:S\ne\varnothing,\ n_S\in\{2,6,12\}\}.
0020: \]
0021: Then $\#\mathcal E_n\le2$, and every member of $\mathcal E_n$ has cardinality
0022: at most two. Define the rank-pure prime sector
0023: \[
0024:  \mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}:=
0025:  \left\{
0026:  \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}p_S:
0027:  \begin{array}{l}
0028:   \mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V),\quad
0029:   \mathcal C\cap\mathcal E_n=\varnothing,\\
0030:   p_S\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)\quad(S\in\mathcal C)
0031:  \end{array}
0032:  \right\}.
0033: \]
0034: Then $\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}\subseteq\mathcal M_n$, the displayed representation is
0035: unique, and
0036: \begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector}
0037:  \#\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}=
0038:  \sum_{\substack{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)\\
0039:                    \mathcal C\cap\mathcal E_n=\varnothing}}
0040:  \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}a_n(S),
0041:  \qquad
0042:  a_n(S)=\sum_{d\mid n_S}\mu(n_S/d)\,\omega(F_d).
0043: \end{equation}
0044: Moreover, the support hypergraph of the product attached to $\mathcal C$ has
0045: edge set exactly $\mathcal C$. In particular, connected minimal covers map to
0046: $\mathcal M_n^{\rm conn}$, with their complete hypergraph structure preserved.
0047: \end{theorem}
0048: 
0049: \begin{proof}
0050: The map $S\mapsto n_S$ is injective. If $n_S=2$, then
0051: $S=\{2\}$ and $\nu_2(n)=1$. If $n_S=6$, then
0052: $S=\{2,3\}$ and $\nu_2(n)=\nu_3(n)=1$; if $n_S=12$, then
0053: $S=\{2,3\}$, $\nu_2(n)=2$, and $\nu_3(n)=1$. Thus the ranks $6$ and $12$
0054: cannot both occur, while rank $2$ can coexist only with rank $6$. This proves
0055: the assertions about $\mathcal E_n$.
0056: 
0057: Fix $\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ avoiding $\mathcal E_n$. For
0058: every $S\in\mathcal C$, the integer $n_S$ is at least $3$ and is not $6$ or
0059: $12$. Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors} therefore gives a prime
0060: $p_S\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)$. Distinct supports have distinct ranks, so the primes
0061: $p_S$ are distinct. Since $p_S$ is a prime jump and $d^-(p_S)=1$,
0062: \[
0063:  E_n(p_S)=T_n(p_S)=S.
0064: \]
0065: Consequently the coverage and private-coordinate conditions defining
0066: $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ are exactly the witness-cover conditions for
0067: $\{p_S:S\in\mathcal C\}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification} places
0068: $\prod_{S\in\mathcal C}p_S$ in $\mathcal M_n$.
0069: 
0070: Unique factorization recovers every selected prime from the product; its rank
0071: $\alpha(p_S)=n_S$ then recovers $S$. Hence both the cover and all prime choices
0072: are recovered, proving injectivity and the weighted count in
0073: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector}. The formula for $a_n(S)$ is
0074: Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}. Finally,
0075: \[
0076:  \operatorname{supp}_n(\alpha(p_S))=
0077:  \operatorname{supp}_n(n_S)=S,
0078: \]
0079: so Definition~\ref{def:support-hypergraph} gives precisely the edge set
0080: $\mathcal C$ and therefore preserves connected components.
0081: \end{proof}
0082: 
0083: \begin{corollary}[Canonical minimal-transversal model]
0084: \label{cor:rank-pure-minimal-transversals}
0085: Retain the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality}. Define a
0086: hypergraph $\mathcal H_n^{\rm rp}$ with vertex set
0087: \[
0088:  U_n:=\{(S,p):\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V,\ S\notin\mathcal E_n,
0089:                     \ p\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)\}
0090: \]
0091: and, for each $\ell\in V$, the coordinate edge
0092: \[
0093:  X_\ell:=\{(S,p)\in U_n:\ell\in S\}.
0094: \]
0095: Multiplication induces a bijection
0096: \begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-pure-minimal-transversal-bijection}
0097:  \operatorname{MinTr}(\mathcal H_n^{\rm rp})
0098:  \longrightarrow \mathcal R_n^{\rm rp},
0099:  \qquad Q\longmapsto\prod_{(S,p)\in Q}p,
0100: \end{equation}
0101: where $\operatorname{MinTr}$ denotes the inclusion-minimal transversals.
0102: Hence the weighted cover polynomial
0103: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector} is exactly a minimal-transversal count of
0104: a canonically defined hypergraph. By the standard split-incidence
0105: correspondence \cite[Proposition~30]{KanteLimouzyMaryNourine2014DominatingSets},
0106: it also counts the minimal connected dominating sets of the associated split
0107: graph.
0108: \end{corollary}
0109: 
0110: \begin{proof}
0111: A set $Q\subseteq U_n$ is a transversal precisely when its support labels
0112: cover $V$. If a minimal transversal contained $(S,p)$ and $(S,q)$ with
0113: $p\ne q$, removing either vertex would preserve every coordinate edge hit by
0114: it, a contradiction. Thus its support labels are distinct. Minimality also
0115: says that every $(S,p)\in Q$ has a coordinate $\ell\in S$ belonging to no
0116: other selected support. The support labels therefore form an irredundant
0117: cover. Conversely, selected prime choices over an irredundant cover form a
0118: minimal transversal, since every selected vertex has such a private
0119: coordinate edge. Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality} and unique
0120: factorization now prove that multiplication is the asserted bijection.
0121: \end{proof}
0122: 
0123: The rank-pure sector has a canonical description on squarefree indices.  In
0124: particular, it is not then an auxiliary class defined only through the cover
0125: construction.
0126: 
0127: \begin{corollary}[Canonical squarefree exact-fiber slice]
0128: \label{cor:canonical-squarefree-slice}
0129: Let $n\ge3$ be squarefree.  Then
0130: \begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-squarefree-slice}
0131:  \mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}
0132:  =\mathcal M_n\cap\{q:\mu^2(q)=1\}
0133:  =\min_{\mid}\{q:\alpha(q)=n,\ \mu^2(q)=1\}.
0134: \end{equation}
0135: Thus the weighted sum in
0136: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector} counts exactly the divisibility-minimal
0137: squarefree elements of the standard exact fiber $\alpha^{-1}(n)$.
0138: \end{corollary}
0139: 
0140: \begin{proof}
0141: Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives
0142: $B_n=\{q:\alpha(q)=n\}=\alpha^{-1}(n)$.  If a squarefree member of $B_n$
0143: has a proper divisor in $B_n$, that divisor is again squarefree.  Hence
0144: minimality in the squarefree part of the exact fiber is equivalent to
0145: membership in $\mathcal M_n$.
0146: 
0147: Every element of $\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}$ is a product of distinct primes and
0148: belongs to $\mathcal M_n$, which proves one inclusion in the first equality.
0149: Conversely, let $m\in\mathcal M_n$ be squarefree.  Its unique rank-jump
0150: factorization from Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification} consists only of
0151: prime jumps $p$.  Put $S=T_n(p)$.  Since $\alpha(p)\mid n$ and $n$ is
0152: squarefree,
0153: \[
0154:  \alpha(p)=\prod_{\ell\in S}\ell=n_S.
0155: \]
0156: Moreover $d^-(p)=1$, so $E_n(p)=T_n(p)=S$.  The witness-cover conditions are
0157: therefore precisely that the distinct supports $S$ form an irredundant cover
0158: of $\mathcal P(n)$.  No such support lies in $\mathcal E_n$, because the
0159: corresponding prime $p$ itself has exact rank $n_S$.  Thus the rank-jump
0160: factorization of $m$ is one of the uniquely represented products defining
0161: $\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}$.  This proves the reverse inclusion and the result.
0162: \end{proof}
0163: 
0164: \subsection*{Worked exact-fiber layers}
0165: 
0166: \begin{example}[An odd squarefree layer without exceptions]
0167: Let $n=15$ and label its prime coordinates by $V=\{3,5\}$. The relevant
0168: Fibonacci factorizations are
0169: \[
0170:  F_3=2,\qquad F_5=5,\qquad F_{15}=2\cdot5\cdot61,
0171: \]
0172: so
0173: \[
0174:  \Pi_\alpha(3)=\{2\},\qquad
0175:  \Pi_\alpha(5)=\{5\},\qquad
0176:  \Pi_\alpha(15)=\{61\}.
0177: \]
0178: There is no exceptional support. For the prime jumps one has
0179: \[
0180:  T_{15}(2)=E_{15}(2)=\{3\},\quad
0181:  T_{15}(5)=E_{15}(5)=\{5\},\quad
0182:  T_{15}(61)=E_{15}(61)=\{3,5\}.
0183: \]
0184: The two irredundant covers of $V$ are
0185: $\{\{3,5\}\}$ and $\{\{3\},\{5\}\}$. They give the products
0186: \[
0187:  61\qquad\text{and}\qquad2\cdot5=10,
0188: \]
0189: respectively. Thus the canonical squarefree slice is
0190: $\mathcal R_{15}^{\rm rp}=\{10,61\}$, with each rank-jump factor, support, essential
0191: support, cover, and product visible in the displays.
0192: \end{example}
0193: 
0194: \begin{example}[An even layer with exceptional supports]
0195: Let $n=6$ and $V=\{2,3\}$. Here the supports $\{2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ carry
0196: the exceptional ranks $2$ and $6$, respectively. The only nonexceptional
0197: support $\{3\}$ cannot cover $V$, so $\mathcal R_6^{\rm rp}=\varnothing$.
0198: On the other hand, $4$ is a ladder jump with
0199: \[
0200:  d(4)=\alpha(4)=6,\qquad d^-(4)=\alpha(2)=3,
0201: \]
0202: and hence
0203: \[
0204:  T_6(4)=\{2,3\},\qquad E_6(4)=\{2\}.
0205: \]
0206: The singleton $\{4\}$ is a witness cover and its product is $4$. Directly,
0207: $F_6=8$ and the ranks of its divisors $1,2,4,8$ are $1,3,6,6$, so
0208: $\mathcal M_6=\{4\}$. This shows exactly how the exceptional support removes
0209: the prime realization while a lowered-label ladder remains.
0210: \end{example}
0211: 
0212: \begin{example}[The ladder boundary at $n=91$]
0213: The coordinates are $V=\{7,13\}$. Since $F_7=13$, one has
0214: $\alpha(13)=7$ and $\nu_{13}(F_7)=1$. Proposition~
0215: \ref{prop:prime-power-ladders} therefore gives
0216: \[
0217:  d(13^2)=\alpha(13^2)=13\alpha(13)=91,
0218:  \qquad d^-(13^2)=7.
0219: \]
0220: Consequently
0221: \[
0222:  T_{91}(169)=\{7,13\},\qquad E_{91}(169)=\{13\}.
0223: \]
0224: The singleton cover $\{169\}$ is irredundant, and its product is $169$, so
0225: $169\in\mathcal M_{91}$. It is a squareful ladder jump and therefore lies
0226: outside the prime-only rank-pure sector:
0227: \[
0228:  169\in\mathcal M_{91}\setminus\mathcal R_{91}^{\rm rp}.
0229: \]
0230: \end{example}
0231: 
0232: \begin{corollary}[Odd-layer cover universality]
0233: \label{cor:odd-rank-pure-universality}
0234: Let $n\ge3$ be odd and put $k=\omega(n)$. Then $\mathcal E_n=\varnothing$.
0235: After fixing one prime $\pi_S\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)$ for every nonempty
0236: $S\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, the map
0237: \[
0238:  \mathcal C\longmapsto\prod_{S\in\mathcal C}\pi_S
0239: \]
0240: embeds $\operatorname{MinCov}(\mathcal P(n))$ into $\mathcal M_n$ and
0241: preserves the support hypergraph. Hence, if $C_k$ denotes the number of minimal
0242: covers of a labelled $k$-set, then
0243: \begin{equation}\label{eq:odd-minimal-cover-bound}
0244:  \#\mathcal M_n\ge C_k,
0245:  \qquad
0246:  \widthop(B_n)\ge C_k.
0247: \end{equation}
0248: Through Royle's correspondence
0249: \cite{Royle2000SetCoversSplitGraphs}, every isomorphism type of split graph on
0250: $k$ vertices consequently has a rank-pure Fibonacci realization on the prime
0251: coordinates of $n$. This last sentence concerns unlabelled isomorphism types
0252: only and is not used to enumerate the labelled covers below.
0253: \end{corollary}
0254: 
0255: \begin{proof}
0256: Every nonempty $n_S$ is odd and at least $3$, so no support is exceptional.
0257: Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality} gives the embedding and support
0258: preservation. Minimal generators form an antichain, which proves the width
0259: bound. Royle's theorem is a correspondence between isomorphism types of split
0260: graphs and minimal covers; choosing a labelling of a representative cover and
0261: then applying the embedding gives the final assertion.
0262: \end{proof}
0263: 
0264: We next fix the classical enumeration input. Let $C_{k,s}$ count the minimal
0265: covers of a labelled $k$-set having
0266: $s$ members, put $C_k=\sum_s C_{k,s}$, and put
0267: \[
0268:  b_k:=\sum_{s=0}^k\binom{k}{s}2^{s(k-s)}.
0269: \]
0270: Hearne and Wagner \cite{HearneWagner1973MinimalCovers} proved
0271: \begin{equation}\label{eq:hearne-wagner}
0272:  C_{k,s}=\sum_{j=s}^k\binom{k}{j}
0273:  \genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{j}{s}
0274:  (2^s-s-1)^{k-j}.
0275: \end{equation}
0276: The prime coordinates of $n$ are specific primes, so the arithmetic embedding
0277: uses these labelled covers: there is no quotient by $S_k$ and no division by
0278: $k!$. Royle's correspondence above concerns isomorphism classes and supplies
0279: only the realization statement. The labelled central sum $b_k$ is the object
0280: in the split-graph enumeration of
0281: Bender--Richmond--Wormald \cite{BenderRichmondWormald1985ChordalSplit}, in the
0282: form recorded by Troyka \cite[Section~3]{Troyka2019SplitGraphs}. The following
0283: direct comparison closes the conversion from the Hearne--Wagner labelled
0284: formula to that labelled central sum.
0285: 
0286: \begin{lemma}[Labelled minimal-cover comparison]
0287: \label{lem:labelled-minimal-cover-comparison}
0288: As $k\to\infty$,
0289: \[
0290:  \frac{C_k}{b_k}\longrightarrow1.
0291: \]
0292: \end{lemma}
0293: 
0294: \begin{proof}
0295: Fix an order on the labelled ground set. In a minimal cover with $s$ members,
0296: select the least private element of each member. The selected elements form an
0297: $s$-set $P$; no selected element can occur in another member, and each member
0298: is recovered from its selected element and a subset of the remaining
0299: $k-s$ elements. This canonical encoding is injective, so
0300: \[
0301:  C_{k,s}\le\binom{k}{s}2^{s(k-s)}.
0302: \]
0303: The $j=s$ term of \eqref{eq:hearne-wagner} gives the matching lower bound
0304: \[
0305:  C_{k,s}\ge\binom{k}{s}(2^s-s-1)^{k-s}.
0306: \]
0307: Uniformly for $k/3\le s\le2k/3$,
0308: \[
0309:  \left(1-\frac{s+1}{2^s}\right)^{k-s}=1-o(1).
0310: \]
0311: The contribution to $b_k$ from the complementary values of $s$ is at most
0312: \[
0313:  2^k2^{2k^2/9}=o\bigl(2^{\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor}\bigr)=o(b_k).
0314: \]
0315: Summing the two bounds over the central range therefore gives
0316: $(1-o(1))b_k\le C_k\le b_k$, which proves the claim.
0317: \end{proof}
0318: 
0319: Consequently, with
0320: \[
0321:  \vartheta_0:=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}2^{-r^2},\qquad
0322:  \vartheta_1:=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}2^{-(r+1/2)^2},\qquad
0323:  \varepsilon\equiv k\pmod2,
0324: \]
0325: the published labelled asymptotic for $b_k$ and
0326: Lemma~\ref{lem:labelled-minimal-cover-comparison} give
0327: \begin{equation}\label{eq:minimal-cover-theta}
0328:  C_k\sim b_k\sim
0329:  \vartheta_\varepsilon\binom{k}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^{k^2/4}.
0330: \end{equation}
0331: In particular, $b_{k-1}/b_k=O(2^{-k/2})$.
0332: 
0333: \begin{corollary}[Weighted-cover obstruction on odd layers]
0334: \label{cor:odd-weighted-cover-obstruction}
0335: Let $n\ge3$ be odd, put $V=\mathcal P(n)$ and $k=\omega(n)$, and retain the
0336: weights $a_n(S)=\#\Pi_\alpha(n_S)$ from
0337: Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality}. Then
0338: \begin{equation}\label{eq:odd-weighted-rank-pure-sector}
0339:  \#\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}
0340:  =\sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
0341:        \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}a_n(S)
0342:  \le\#\mathcal M_n.
0343: \end{equation}
0344: Every weight in this sum is positive. Consequently, with
0345: \begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-cover-excess}
0346:  \mathcal W(n):=\frac1{C_k}
0347:  \sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
0348:        \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}a_n(S)\ge1,
0349: \end{equation}
0350: one has
0351: \begin{equation}\label{eq:odd-rank-pure-log-decomposition}
0352:  \log\#\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}
0353:  =\frac{\log2}{4}k^2+\log\mathcal W(n)+O(k).
0354: \end{equation}
0355: Therefore an almost-all asymptotic
0356: \[
0357:  \log\#\mathcal M_n\sim\frac{\log2}{4}(\log\log n)^2
0358: \]
0359: would necessarily imply
0360: \begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-cover-dispersion-interface}
0361:  \log\mathcal W(n)=o\bigl((\log\log n)^2\bigr)
0362: \end{equation}
0363: outside an $o(x)$ exceptional set of odd $n\le x$.
0364: The converse is not asserted: ladder jumps and other non-rank-pure witness
0365: covers still require an upper bound.  This distinction occurs already at the
0366: odd squarefree index $91$, where $\alpha(13)=7$ and
0367: $\alpha(13^2)=91$, so $169\in\mathcal M_{91}\setminus\mathcal R_{91}^{\rm rp}$.
0368: \end{corollary}
0369: 
0370: \begin{proof}
0371: For odd $n$, every $n_S$ is odd and at least $3$, so
0372: $\mathcal E_n=\varnothing$ and the exact-rank existence theorem gives
0373: $a_n(S)\ge1$.  The weighted identity and inclusion are
0374: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector}.  The asymptotic
0375: \eqref{eq:minimal-cover-theta} gives
0376: $\log C_k=(\log2)k^2/4+O(k)$ and proves
0377: \eqref{eq:odd-rank-pure-log-decomposition}.
0378: 
0379: If the displayed almost-all formula for $\mathcal M_n$ held, then it would
0380: hold outside an $o(x)$ subset of the odd integers.  Intersecting with the
0381: Hardy--Ramanujan normal-order set and using
0382: $\#\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}\le\#\mathcal M_n$ forces
0383: \eqref{eq:weighted-cover-dispersion-interface}.  Finally, the classical
0384: lifting formula gives $\alpha(13^2)=13\alpha(13)=91$ and
0385: $\alpha(13)=7<91$.  Thus $13^2$ is a rank-jump factor of rank $91$ and the singleton
0386: witness cover $\{13^2\}$ gives the stated strict inclusion.
0387: \end{proof}
0388: 
0389: The following sharp extremal calculation separates total primitive-prime
0390: mass from the dispersion information retained by the cover polynomial.
0391: 
0392: \begin{proposition}[Sharp cumulative-data obstruction]
0393: \label{prop:sharp-cumulative-data-obstruction}
0394: Let $V$ be a labelled $k$-set, $k\ge1$, and assign a real weight
0395: $w_S\ge1$ to every nonempty $S\subseteq V$.  Put
0396: \[
0397:  Z_V(w):=\sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
0398:               \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}w_S,
0399:  \qquad A:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}w_S.
0400: \]
0401: Then
0402: \begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}
0403:  Z_V(w)\ge C_k+A-(2^k-1).
0404: \end{equation}
0405: This is best possible for every $A\ge2^k-1$: equality is attained by
0406: \[
0407:  w_V=A-(2^k-2),\qquad w_S=1\quad(S\ne V).
0408: \]
0409: If $k\ge3$, this is the only equality profile.
0410: 
0411: Consequently, if $n\ge3$ is odd and squarefree and $k=\omega(n)$, then
0412: \begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-rank-pure-bound}
0413:  \#\{m\in\mathcal M_n:\mu^2(m)=1\}
0414:  \ge C_k+\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1),
0415: \end{equation}
0416: and
0417: \begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-weighted-excess}
0418:  \mathcal W(n)\ge
0419:  1+\frac{\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1)}{C_k}.
0420: \end{equation}
0421: Among all positive weight profiles with the same total
0422: $\sum_{d\mid n,\ d>1}a(d)=\omega(F_n)$, this conclusion is exact.  The
0423: extremizing profile is an abstract information-theoretic model; it is not
0424: asserted to be realized by Fibonacci exact-rank primes.
0425: \end{proposition}
0426: 
0427: \begin{proof}
0428: Write $w_S=1+x_S$ with $x_S\ge0$.  For every minimal cover $\mathcal C$,
0429: \[
0430:  \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}(1+x_S)
0431:  \ge1+\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}x_S.
0432: \]
0433: Every nonempty $S\subseteq V$ occurs in a minimal cover: use $\{V\}$ when
0434: $S=V$, and otherwise use
0435: $\{S\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V\setminus S\}$.  Summing the preceding inequality
0436: over all minimal covers therefore gives
0437: \[
0438:  Z_V(w)\ge C_k+\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}x_S
0439:  =C_k+A-(2^k-1).
0440: \]
0441: The only minimal cover containing $V$ is $\{V\}$.  Hence the displayed
0442: full-support profile has weighted sum
0443: $C_k-1+w_V=C_k+A-(2^k-1)$, proving sharpness.
0444: 
0445: Suppose $k\ge3$ and $S$ is proper and nonempty. If $|S|=1$, both the
0446: singleton partition of $V$ and $\{S,V\setminus S\}$ are minimal covers
0447: containing $S$. If $|S|\ge2$, choose $s\in S$ and $t\in V\setminus S$; in
0448: addition to the preceding singleton-complement cover, there is the minimal
0449: cover consisting of $S$, $\{s,t\}$, and the singletons
0450: $\{v\}$ for $v\in V\setminus(S\cup\{t\})$. Thus every proper $S$ occurs in
0451: at least two minimal covers. In the summed linear lower bound its coefficient
0452: is therefore at least two, so equality forces $x_S=0$ for every proper $S$.
0453: This proves the equality classification.
0454: 
0455: For odd squarefree $n$, the nonempty subsets of $\mathcal P(n)$ correspond
0456: to the divisors $d>1$ of $n$.  Exact ranks partition the prime divisors of
0457: $F_n$, and $a(1)=0$, so
0458: \[
0459:  \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}a(n_S)
0460:  =\sum_{d\mid n}a(d)=\omega(F_n).
0461: \]
0462: Every weight is positive by exact-rank prime existence.  Apply
0463: \eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}, then use
0464: Corollary~\ref{cor:canonical-squarefree-slice} and
0465: \eqref{eq:weighted-cover-excess}.
0466: \end{proof}

0063: \begin{corollary}[Rank-jump prime-power classification]
0064: \label{cor:rank-jump-classification}
0065: The rank-jump prime powers are exactly the following:
0066: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
0067: \item $2\in\Atom(3)$, $4\in\Atom(6)$, and
0068: $2^e\in\Atom(3\cdot2^{e-2})$ for every $e\ge4$; the power $8$ is not
0069: rank-jump.
0070: \item $5^e\in\Atom(5^e)$ for every $e\ge1$.
0071: \item If $p\ne2,5$, $z_p=\alpha(p)$, and
0072: $h_p=\nu_p(F_{z_p})$, then $p\in\Atom(z_p)$ and
0073: $p^e\in\Atom(p^{e-h_p}z_p)$ for every $e>h_p$; no power $p^e$ with
0074: $1<e\le h_p$ is rank-jump.
0075: \end{enumerate}
0076: Consequently every rank-jump factor is either a prime jump or a ladder jump $p^e$ with
0077: $e>1$. Every ladder step changes only the $p$-adic coordinate of its
0078: apparition index when it is lowered to $p^{e-1}$.
0079: \end{corollary}
0080: 
0081: \begin{proof}
0082: Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders}. For $p=2$, the ranks are
0083: $3,6,6,12,24,\ldots$ on $2,4,8,16,32,\ldots$. For $p=5$, every step is
0084: rank-jump. If $p\ne2,5$, the rank remains $z_p$ for $1\le e\le h_p$ and then
0085: gains one factor of $p$ at each further level. The last assertion follows
0086: from the same formulas.
0087: \end{proof}
0088: 
0089: \begin{lemma}[Prime-ladder dichotomy]
0090: \label{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}
0091: Let $\theta=p^e\in\Atom(d)$ and suppose $d\mid n$. If $e=1$, then
0092: \[
0093: E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta).
0094: \]
0095: If $e>1$, then $E_n(\theta)$ is either empty or the singleton $\{p\}$.
0096: In particular, no Fibonacci rank-jump factor has
0097: \[
0098: 1<\#E_n(\theta)<\#T_n(\theta).
0099: \]
0100: \end{lemma}
0101: 
0102: \begin{proof}
0103: If $e=1$, then $d^-(\theta)=\alpha(1)=1$, so every coordinate in
0104: $T_n(\theta)$ is lost after lowering. Assume $e>1$. By
0105: Corollary~\ref{cor:rank-jump-classification}, $\theta$ is a ladder jump.
0106: Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders} shows that $d(\theta)$ and
0107: $d^-(\theta)$ differ only in their $p$-adic coordinate. Therefore the only
0108: full coordinate that can be lost is $p$ itself, and the result follows.
0109: \end{proof}
0110: 
0111: For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, define the prime window
0112: \[
0113: P_J(n):=\coprod_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)=J}}\Pi_\alpha(d),
0114: \]
0115: where $T_n(d)=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):
0116: \nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}$.  A prime in $P_J(n)$ is identified with its
0117: prime jump.
0118: 
0119: \begin{proposition}[Rank-jump families and unique ladder slots]
0120: \label{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots}
0121: Let $n\ge3$ and let $\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$.
0122: Then every rank-jump factor in $\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)$ is either in the prime window
0123: $P_J(n)$, which occurs only when $I=J$, or in a ladder family with
0124: $I=\{p\}$ for a prime coordinate $p\in J$.  Each such ladder family contains
0125: at most one rank-jump factor.
0126: 
0127: More precisely, put $a=\nu_p(n)$.  Its only possible ladder jump is
0128: \[
0129: \lambda_p(n)=
0130: \begin{cases}
0131: 4, & p=2,\ a=1,\\
0132: 2^{a+2}, & p=2,\ a\ge2,\\
0133: 5^a, & p=5,\ a\ge2,\\
0134: p^{h_p+a}, & p\notin\{2,5\},
0135: \end{cases}
0136: \]
0137: with no candidate for $p=5$, $a=1$.  The candidate belongs to
0138: $\mathcal A_{\{p\},J}(n)$ exactly when
0139: $d(\lambda_p(n))\mid n$ and $T_n(\lambda_p(n))=J$.
0140: Consequently every rank-jump family is finite, every nonsingleton rank-jump family
0141: is a finite disjoint union of exact-rank prime classes, and every labelled
0142: ladder slot has at most one candidate.
0143: \end{proposition}
0144: 
0145: \begin{proof}
0146: If $\theta=q$ is a prime jump, the prime-ladder dichotomy gives
0147: $E_n(q)=T_n(q)$, and $q$ belongs to the unique class
0148: $\Pi_\alpha(d(q))$ in $P_{T_n(q)}(n)$. Conversely every prime in $P_J(n)$
0149: has $(E_n,T_n)=(J,J)$.
0150: 
0151: Suppose $\theta=q^e$ is a ladder jump. The same dichotomy gives
0152: $E_n(\theta)=\{q\}$ whenever the essential support is nonempty. Hence its
0153: essential coordinate determines its underlying prime, so $q=p$. The
0154: full-exponent equation
0155: $\nu_p(d(p^e))=\nu_p(n)=a$ and
0156: Proposition~\ref{prop:prime-power-ladders} now leave only the displayed
0157: candidate. For $p=2$, the rank-jump ladder levels are $4$ of rank $6$ and
0158: $2^e$ of rank $3\cdot2^{e-2}$ for $e\ge4$. For $p=5$, the rank is $5^e$,
0159: and $e=1$ is a prime jump. For $p\notin\{2,5\}$, one has
0160: $p\nmid z_p$ and
0161: $\alpha(p^e)=p^{e-h_p}z_p$ at rank-jump ladder levels, so $e=h_p+a$.
0162: The remaining conditions $d(\theta)\mid n$ and $T_n(\theta)=J$ are exactly
0163: the conditions for membership in $\mathcal A_{\{p\},J}(n)$.
0164: 
0165: Finally, each $\Pi_\alpha(d)$ is finite by
0166: Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}, and there are only finitely many
0167: divisors $d$ of $n$. This proves all finiteness and uniqueness assertions.
0168: \end{proof}

0001: \section{Rank-pure covers and the canonical squarefree slice}
0002: \label{sec:rank-pure}
0003: 
0004: For a finite set $V$, write $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ for the set of
0005: irredundant covers of $V$ by distinct nonempty subsets: a family
0006: $\mathcal C$ belongs to $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ when
0007: $\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal C}S=V$ and every $S\in\mathcal C$ contains an element
0008: outside $\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal C\setminus\{S\}}T$.
0009: 
0010: \begin{theorem}[Rank-pure universality]\label{thm:rank-pure-universality}
0011: Let $n\ge3$, put $V=\mathcal P(n)$, and, for every nonempty $S\subseteq V$,
0012: define
0013: \[
0014:  n_S:=\prod_{\ell\in S}\ell^{\nu_\ell(n)},\qquad
0015:  a_n(S):=\#\Pi_\alpha(n_S),
0016: \]
0017: and
0018: \[
0019:  \mathcal E_n:=\{S\subseteq V:S\ne\varnothing,\ n_S\in\{2,6,12\}\}.
0020: \]
0021: Then $\#\mathcal E_n\le2$, and every member of $\mathcal E_n$ has cardinality
0022: at most two. Define the rank-pure prime sector
0023: \[
0024:  \mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}:=
0025:  \left\{
0026:  \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}p_S:
0027:  \begin{array}{l}
0028:   \mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V),\quad
0029:   \mathcal C\cap\mathcal E_n=\varnothing,\\
0030:   p_S\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)\quad(S\in\mathcal C)
0031:  \end{array}
0032:  \right\}.
0033: \]
0034: Then $\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}\subseteq\mathcal M_n$, the displayed representation is
0035: unique, and
0036: \begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector}
0037:  \#\mathcal R_n^{\rm rp}=
0038:  \sum_{\substack{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)\\
0039:                    \mathcal C\cap\mathcal E_n=\varnothing}}
0040:  \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}a_n(S),
0041:  \qquad
0042:  a_n(S)=\sum_{d\mid n_S}\mu(n_S/d)\,\omega(F_d).
0043: \end{equation}
0044: Moreover, the support hypergraph of the product attached to $\mathcal C$ has
0045: edge set exactly $\mathcal C$. In particular, connected minimal covers map to
0046: $\mathcal M_n^{\rm conn}$, with their complete hypergraph structure preserved.
0047: \end{theorem}
0048: 
0049: \begin{proof}
0050: The map $S\mapsto n_S$ is injective. If $n_S=2$, then
0051: $S=\{2\}$ and $\nu_2(n)=1$. If $n_S=6$, then
0052: $S=\{2,3\}$ and $\nu_2(n)=\nu_3(n)=1$; if $n_S=12$, then
0053: $S=\{2,3\}$, $\nu_2(n)=2$, and $\nu_3(n)=1$. Thus the ranks $6$ and $12$
0054: cannot both occur, while rank $2$ can coexist only with rank $6$. This proves
0055: the assertions about $\mathcal E_n$.
0056: 
0057: Fix $\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ avoiding $\mathcal E_n$. For
0058: every $S\in\mathcal C$, the integer $n_S$ is at least $3$ and is not $6$ or
0059: $12$. Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors} therefore gives a prime
0060: $p_S\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)$. Distinct supports have distinct ranks, so the primes
0061: $p_S$ are distinct. Since $p_S$ is a prime jump and $d^-(p_S)=1$,
0062: \[
0063:  E_n(p_S)=T_n(p_S)=S.
0064: \]
0065: Consequently the coverage and private-coordinate conditions defining
0066: $\operatorname{MinCov}(V)$ are exactly the witness-cover conditions for
0067: $\{p_S:S\in\mathcal C\}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification} places
0068: $\prod_{S\in\mathcal C}p_S$ in $\mathcal M_n$.
0069: 
0070: Unique factorization recovers every selected prime from the product; its rank
0071: $\alpha(p_S)=n_S$ then recovers $S$. Hence both the cover and all prime choices
0072: are recovered, proving injectivity and the weighted count in
0073: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector}. The formula for $a_n(S)$ is
0074: Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}. Finally,
0075: \[
0076:  \operatorname{supp}_n(\alpha(p_S))=
0077:  \operatorname{supp}_n(n_S)=S,
0078: \]
0079: so Definition~\ref{def:support-hypergraph} gives precisely the edge set
0080: $\mathcal C$ and therefore preserves connected components.
0081: \end{proof}
0082: 
0083: \begin{corollary}[Canonical minimal-transversal model]
0084: \label{cor:rank-pure-minimal-transversals}
0085: Retain the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality}. Define a
0086: hypergraph $\mathcal H_n^{\rm rp}$ with vertex set
0087: \[
0088:  U_n:=\{(S,p):\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V,\ S\notin\mathcal E_n,
0089:                     \ p\in\Pi_\alpha(n_S)\}
0090: \]
0091: and, for each $\ell\in V$, the coordinate edge
0092: \[
0093:  X_\ell:=\{(S,p)\in U_n:\ell\in S\}.
0094: \]
0095: Multiplication induces a bijection
0096: \begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-pure-minimal-transversal-bijection}
0097:  \operatorname{MinTr}(\mathcal H_n^{\rm rp})
0098:  \longrightarrow \mathcal R_n^{\rm rp},
0099:  \qquad Q\longmapsto\prod_{(S,p)\in Q}p,
0100: \end{equation}
0101: where $\operatorname{MinTr}$ denotes the inclusion-minimal transversals.
0102: Hence the weighted cover polynomial
0103: \eqref{eq:rank-pure-weighted-sector} is exactly a minimal-transversal count of
0104: a canonically defined hypergraph. By the standard split-incidence
0105: correspondence \cite[Proposition~30]{KanteLimouzyMaryNourine2014DominatingSets},
0106: it also counts the minimal connected dominating sets of the associated split
0107: graph.
0108: \end{corollary}
0109: 
0110: \begin{proof}
0111: A set $Q\subseteq U_n$ is a transversal precisely when its support labels
0112: cover $V$. If a minimal transversal contained $(S,p)$ and $(S,q)$ with
0113: $p\ne q$, removing either vertex would preserve every coordinate edge hit by
0114: it, a contradiction. Thus its support labels are distinct. Minimality also
0115: says that every $(S,p)\in Q$ has a coordinate $\ell\in S$ belonging to no
0116: other selected support. The support labels therefore form an irredundant
0117: cover. Conversely, selected prime choices over an irredundant cover form a
0118: minimal transversal, since every selected vertex has such a private
0119: coordinate edge. Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-pure-universality} and unique
0120: factorization now prove that multiplication is the asserted bijection.
0121: \end{proof}

0124: particular, it is not then an auxiliary class defined only through the cover
0125: construction.

0001: \section{Support entropy and the unresolved arithmetic multiplicity}
0002: \label{sec:growth}
0003: %% ====================================================================
0004: 
0005: Write $\Omega(N)=\sum_p\nu_p(N)$ for the number of prime factors of $N$
0006: counted with multiplicity. Set $R(2)=1$, consistently with
0007: $\mathcal M_2=\varnothing$. For $n\ge3$ define the maximal rank-window
0008: multiplicity
0009: \begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-window-multiplicity}
0010:  R(n):=\max\!\left\{1,
0011:  \max_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}
0012:        \#\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)\right\}.
0013: \end{equation}
0014: By the prime--ladder alternative, the nonsingleton families counted here are the
0015: exact-rank windows $P_J(n)$, whereas every ladder family contributes at most
0016: one rank-jump factor. Thus $R(n)$ records the maximal rank-jump-family multiplicity retained
0017: by the counting bounds below. It is an exact parameter for those bounds, but
0018: it is not asserted to be an information-theoretically complete invariant of
0019: the arithmetic outside the support combinatorics.
0020: 
0021: We first remove the contribution caused solely by collecting several exact
0022: rank classes in one support window. For $d\mid n$, write
0023: \[
0024:  T_n(d):=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):
0025:  \nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}.
0026: \]
0027: 
0028: \begin{theorem}[Mean rank-window deaggregation]
0029: \label{thm:mean-rank-window-deaggregation}
0030: Put
0031: \[
0032:  a(d):=\#\Pi_\alpha(d),\qquad
0033:  \mathcal D^+(n):=\{d\mid n:T_n(d)\ne\varnothing\},
0034: \]
0035: and
0036: \[
0037:  A^*(n):=\max\left\{1,\max_{d\in\mathcal D^+(n)}a(d)\right\}.
0038: \]
0039: Then, as $x\to\infty$,
0040: \begin{equation}\label{eq:mean-window-deaggregation}
0041:  \sum_{3\le n\le x}\omega(n)\log R(n)
0042:  =\sum_{3\le n\le x}\omega(n)\log A^*(n)
0043:  +O(x\log\log x).
0044: \end{equation}
0045: Consequently the mean sparse-window hypothesis \textup{(H2)} is equivalent to
0046: \begin{equation}\label{eq:visible-single-rank-interface}
0047:  \sum_{3\le n\le x}\omega(n)
0048:  \log\max\left\{1,
0049:  \max_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)\ne\varnothing}}
0050:  \#\Pi_\alpha(d)\right\}
0051:  =o\bigl(x(\log\log x)^2\bigr).
0052: \end{equation}
0053: \end{theorem}
0054: 
0055: \begin{proof}
0056: For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, let
0057: \[
0058:  W_J(n):=\{d\mid n:T_n(d)=J\}.
0059: \]
0060: If $n=\prod_\ell\ell^{e_\ell}$, then
0061: \begin{equation}\label{eq:support-window-size}
0062:  \#W_J(n)=\prod_{\ell\notin J}e_\ell.
0063: \end{equation}
0064: The prime jumps in the family with essential and full supports $(J,J)$ form
0065: the finite disjoint union
0066: \[
0067:  \coprod_{d\in W_J(n)}\Pi_\alpha(d),
0068: \]
0069: because a prime has a unique rank of apparition. By the prime--ladder
0070: alternative and the unique ladder-slot formula in
0071: Lemma~\ref{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy} and
0072: Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots}, every remaining effective
0073: rank-jump family is a ladder family with singleton essential support and at most
0074: one rank-jump factor. Therefore, with
0075: \[
0076:  P(n):=\max_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}
0077:        \sum_{d\in W_J(n)}a(d),
0078: \]
0079: one has
0080: \begin{equation}\label{eq:prime-window-versus-R}
0081:  P(n)\le R(n)\le P(n)+1.
0082: \end{equation}
0083: Every $d\in\mathcal D^+(n)$ belongs to one of the windows above. Hence
0084: \[
0085:  A^*(n)\le R(n)
0086:  \le1+A^*(n)\max_J\#W_J(n)
0087:  \le1+A^*(n)\prod_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}e_\ell.
0088: \]
0089: Writing
0090: \[
0091:  h(n):=\sum_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}\log e_\ell,
0092: \]
0093: and using $A^*(n)\ge1$ gives
0094: \begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}
0095:  0\le\log R(n)-\log A^*(n)\le\log2+h(n).
0096: \end{equation}
0097: For each exponent $e\ge2$, $\log e\le\sum_{2\le j\le e}\log j$, so
0098: \[
0099:  h(n)\le\sum_{\substack{p^j\mid n\\j\ge2}}\log j.
0100: \]
0101: The classical mean estimate \eqref{eq:mean-omega-input}, used uniformly with
0102: $\log\log(3y)$ in place of $\log\log y$ for small $y$, yields
0103: \begin{align*}
0104:  \sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)h(n)
0105:  &\le\sum_{\substack{p^j\le x\\j\ge2}}\log j
0106:        \sum_{m\le x/p^j}\omega(p^jm)\\
0107:  &\le\sum_{\substack{p^j\le x\\j\ge2}}\log j
0108:        \sum_{m\le x/p^j}(1+\omega(m))\\
0109:  &\ll x\log\log x\sum_p\sum_{j\ge2}\frac{\log j}{p^j}
0110:  \ll x\log\log x.
0111: \end{align*}
0112: The double series converges absolutely. Summing
0113: \eqref{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation} and using
0114: $\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)\ll x\log\log x$ proves
0115: \eqref{eq:mean-window-deaggregation}; the stated equivalence follows because
0116: $x\log\log x=o(x(\log\log x)^2)$.
0117: \end{proof}

0119: \begin{corollary}[Single-rank sufficient and necessary interfaces]
0120: \label{cor:single-rank-mean-interfaces}
0121: A sufficient condition for \textup{(H2)} is
0122: \begin{equation}\label{eq:single-rank-sufficient-condition}
0123:  \sum_{d\le x}
0124:  \frac{(\omega(d)+\log\log x)\log\max\{1,a(d)\}}{d}
0125:  =o\bigl((\log\log x)^2\bigr).
0126: \end{equation}
0127: Conversely, \textup{(H2)} implies the diagonal necessary condition
0128: \begin{equation}\label{eq:single-rank-necessary-condition}
0129:  \sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)\log\max\{1,a(n)\}
0130:  =o\bigl(x(\log\log x)^2\bigr).
0131: \end{equation}
0132: \end{corollary}
0133: 
0134: \begin{proof}
0135: Since
0136: \[
0137:  \log A^*(n)\le\sum_{d\mid n}\log\max\{1,a(d)\},
0138: \]
0139: the substitution $n=dm$ and $\omega(dm)\le\omega(d)+\omega(m)$ gives
0140: \[
0141:  \sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)\log A^*(n)
0142:  \ll x\sum_{d\le x}
0143:  \frac{(\omega(d)+\log\log x)\log\max\{1,a(d)\}}{d}.
0144: \]
0145: Thus \eqref{eq:single-rank-sufficient-condition} and
0146: Theorem~\ref{thm:mean-rank-window-deaggregation} imply \textup{(H2)}. For the
0147: necessary condition, $n\in\mathcal D^+(n)$, and hence
0148: $R(n)\ge A^*(n)\ge\max\{1,a(n)\}$; summation proves the claim.
0149: \end{proof}

0151: The Fibonacci polynomials were studied by Webb--Parberry
0152: \cite{WebbParberry1969FibonacciPolynomials}; Levy introduced the fibotomic
0153: polynomials and proved their irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$
0154: \cite{Levy2001FibonacciPolynomials}; and Byer--Dvorachek--Eckard--Harrington--
0155: Wise--Wong developed their later systematic theory
0156: \cite{CameronCountsLundMillerPiechnikWong2022Fibotomic}. We use only the
0157: definition and factorization identity recorded in the following lemma.
0158: Thus $\Psi_d(1)$ is the standard Fibonacci cyclotomic, or fibotomic,
0159: integer; only the notation $\mathfrak F_d$ below is local to this paper.
0160: 
0161: \begin{lemma}[Fibotomic integer and exact-rank radical]
0162: \label{lem:fibotomic-integer-radical}
0163: Let $d\ge3$, let $\Psi_d(x)$ be the $d$th fibotomic polynomial, and put
0164: \[
0165:  \mathfrak F_d:=\prod_{r\mid d}F_r^{\mu(d/r)}.
0166: \]
0167: Then
0168: \begin{equation}\label{eq:fibotomic-integer-identity}
0169:  \mathfrak F_d=\Psi_d(1)\in\mathbb N,
0170: \end{equation}
0171: and
0172: \begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-rank-radical-divides-fibotomic}
0173:  \prod_{p\in\Pi_\alpha(d)}p\mid\mathfrak F_d.
0174: \end{equation}
0175: For $d=3,5$ the exact-rank radicals are respectively $2$ and $5$; for
0176: $d=6,12$ the exact-rank layer is empty, so the product in the second display
0177: is $1$.
0178: \end{lemma}
0179: 
0180: \begin{proof}
0181: The polynomial factorization
0182: \[
0183:  F_d(x)=\prod_{r\mid d}\Psi_r(x)
0184: \]
0185: and M\"obius inversion in the multiplicative group of nonzero rational
0186: functions give
0187: \[
0188:  \Psi_d(x)=\prod_{r\mid d}F_r(x)^{\mu(d/r)}.
0189: \]
0190: Evaluation at $x=1$ proves
0191: $\mathfrak F_d=\Psi_d(1)$. The fibotomic polynomial has positive integral
0192: value at $1$, proving \eqref{eq:fibotomic-integer-identity} despite the
0193: negative exponents in the M\"obius expression.
0194: 
0195: If $p\in\Pi_\alpha(d)$, then $p\mid F_d$ but $p\nmid F_r$ for every proper
0196: divisor $r$ of $d$. In the integral factorization
0197: $F_d=\prod_{r\mid d}\Psi_r(1)$, any divisibility
0198: $p\mid\Psi_r(1)$ with $r<d$ would imply $p\mid F_r$, because
0199: $\Psi_r(1)\mid F_r$. Hence $p\mid\Psi_d(1)=\mathfrak F_d$. Distinct
0200: exact-rank primes are coprime, which proves the radical divisibility without
0201: any appeal to cancellation in the M\"obius quotient. The small-rank claims
0202: follow from $\alpha(2)=3$, $\alpha(5)=5$, and the absence of exact-rank
0203: primes at ranks $6$ and $12$.
0204: \end{proof}

0206: \begin{theorem}[Fibotomic rank entropy]
0207: \label{thm:fibotomic-rank-entropy}
0208: Let $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$, let $\phi_{\rm E}$ denote Euler's totient
0209: function, and, for $d\geq3$, put
0210: \[
0211:  \mathfrak F_d:=\prod_{r\mid d}F_r^{\mu(d/r)}.
0212: \]
0213: For $k\geq0$, set $m=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$ and
0214: \[
0215:  \mathcal H_d(k):=
0216:  k\log\frac{2d}{3}+2\log(m!)+(k-2m)\log(m+1).
0217: \]
0218: There is an absolute constant $C_F$ such that, for every $d\geq3$,
0219: \begin{equation}\label{eq:fibotomic-rank-entropy}
0220:  \mathcal H_d(a(d))\leq \phi_{\rm E}(d)\log\varphi+C_F.
0221: \end{equation}
0222: More generally, every finitely supported family of nonnegative real numbers
0223: $(\lambda_d)_{d\geq3}$ satisfies
0224: \begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-fibotomic-rank-entropy}
0225:  \sum_{d\geq3}\lambda_d\mathcal H_d(a(d))
0226:  \leq (\log\varphi)\sum_{d\geq3}\lambda_d\phi_{\rm E}(d)
0227:        +C_F\sum_{d\geq3}\lambda_d.
0228: \end{equation}
0229: Uniformly as $d\to\infty$,
0230: \begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-exact-rank-bound}
0231:  a(d)\leq
0232:  \left(\frac{\log\varphi}{2}+o(1)\right)
0233:  \frac{\phi_{\rm E}(d)}{\log d}.
0234: \end{equation}
0235: Consequently, uniformly as $n\to\infty$,
0236: \begin{equation}\label{eq:visible-exact-rank-bound}
0237:  A^*(n)\leq
0238:  \left(\frac{\log\varphi}{2}+o(1)\right)
0239:  \frac{\phi_{\rm E}(n)}{\log n}.
0240: \end{equation}
0241: \end{theorem}
0242: 
0243: \begin{proof}
0244: Binet's formula, in the form
0245: \[
0246:  F_r=\frac{\varphi^r}{\sqrt5}
0247:  \bigl(1-(-\varphi^{-2})^r\bigr),
0248: \]
0249: and the identities
0250: $\sum_{r\mid d}\mu(d/r)=0$ and
0251: $\sum_{r\mid d}r\mu(d/r)=\phi_{\rm E}(d)$ show that
0252: \begin{equation}\label{eq:fibotomic-binet-error}
0253:  \log\mathfrak F_d=\phi_{\rm E}(d)\log\varphi+E_d,
0254:  \qquad
0255:  |E_d|\leq
0256:  C_F:=\sum_{j\geq1}
0257:  \left|\log\bigl(1-(-\varphi^{-2})^j\bigr)\right|.
0258: \end{equation}
0259: The series defining $C_F$ converges geometrically.
0260:

0001: \begin{theorem}[Multiplicity-free support entropy with arithmetic remainder]
0002: \label{thm:minimal-generator-growth}
0003: For every integer $n\ge3$, put $k=\omega(n)$ and
0004: $L(n)=\log\#\mathcal M_n$. Then $\mathcal M_n$ is nonempty. If $k\ge3$ and
0005: $r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, then
0006: \begin{equation}\label{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}
0007:  (2^r-1)^{k-r}
0008:  \le \#\mathcal M_n
0009:  \le \sum_{s=1}^{k}\binom{k}{s}(2R(n))^s2^{s(k-s)}.
0010: \end{equation}
0011: In particular, uniformly along every sequence for which $\omega(n)\to\infty$,
0012: \begin{equation}\label{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}
0013:  \frac{\log2}{4}\,\omega(n)^2-O(1)
0014:  \le L(n)
0015:  \le \frac{\log2}{4}\,\omega(n)^2
0016:       +\omega(n)\log R(n)+O(\omega(n)).
0017: \end{equation}
0018: No exact quadratic coefficient for the full quantity $L(n)$ is claimed.
0019: The coefficient $\log2/4$ is exact only for the multiplicity-free
0020: minimal-cover contribution: the lower construction embeds the unweighted
0021: cover count, and the private-coordinate encoding gives the same quadratic
0022: support term in the upper bound. The display is not an asymptotic formula for
0023: $L(n)$ unless $R(n)=\exp(o(\omega(n)))$; no such unconditional estimate for
0024: $R(n)$ is proved here. In particular, the displayed coefficient is not
0025: claimed to be optimal among all deductions from fibotomic or exact-rank
0026: arithmetic information.
0027: 
0028: For comparison, the crude support-count estimate gives
0029: \begin{equation}
0030: \label{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}
0031:  \#\mathcal M_n
0032:  \le \sum_{r=0}^{k}\binom{\Omega(F_n)}{r}
0033:  \le n^k.
0034: \end{equation}
0035: Combining only the last inequality with the classical maximal order of
0036: $\omega(n)$ gives the crude corollary
0037: \begin{equation}
0038: \label{eq:crude-maximal-order}
0039:  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
0040:  \frac{L(n)\log\log n}{(\log n)^2}\le1.
0041: \end{equation}
0042: This envelope has scale $(\log n)^2/\log\log n$, a factor $\log\log n$
0043: above the witness-cover entropy scale; it is not a consequence of
0044: \eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}.
0045: At the coarser divisor-lattice scale, the antichain property and Wigert's
0046: theorem give the Sperner-type envelope
0047: \begin{equation}
0048: \label{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}
0049:  L(n)\le\log\tau(F_n)
0050:  \le (\log2\,\log\varphi+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n},
0051:  \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2};
0052: \end{equation}
0053: in fact \eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order} is stronger and implies
0054: $L(n)=o(n/\log n)$.
0055: 
0056: Moreover, as $x\to\infty$,
0057: \begin{equation}
0058: \label{eq:mean-logarithmic-growth}
0059:  \left(\frac{\log2}{4}+o(1)\right)x(\log\log x)^2
0060:  \le \sum_{3\le n\le x}L(n)
0061:  \le (1+o(1))x\log x\,\log\log x.
0062: \end{equation}
0063: 
0064: \end{theorem}
0065: 
0066: \begin{proof}
0067: First, $F_n\in B_n$ for every $n\ge3$.  Indeed,
0068: $F_n\mid F_d$ implies $F_n\le F_d$, and strict increase of the Fibonacci
0069: sequence from index $2$ onward forces $d\ge n$; hence $\alpha(F_n)=n$.
0070: Because $B_n$ is a nonempty finite poset, it has a minimal element, so
0071: $\mathcal M_n\ne\varnothing$ and $L(n)$ is defined.
0072: 
0073: We first prove the explicit finite private-cover bound in
0074: \eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}. Fix $k\ge3$, and give
0075: $\mathcal P(n)$ an arbitrary order. Put
0076: \[
0077:  X=\mathcal P(n)\cap\{2,3\},\qquad r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor.
0078: \]
0079: Since $k-\#X\ge k-2\ge r$, choose an $r$-element set
0080: $P\subseteq\mathcal P(n)\setminus X$, and put
0081: $Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. For every map
0082: \[
0083:  H:Q\longrightarrow 2^P\setminus\{\varnothing\}
0084: \]
0085: and every $i\in P$, define
0086: \[
0087:  T_i=\{i\}\cup\{q\in Q:i\in H(q)\}.
0088: \]
0089: The index $n_{T_i}=\prod_{\ell\in T_i}\ell^{\nu_\ell(n)}$ has a prime
0090: divisor outside $\{2,3\}$, because $i\in P$. Hence $n_{T_i}\ge5$ and
0091: $n_{T_i}\notin\{6,12\}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors} supplies a
0092: prime $\pi_{T_i}$ with $\alpha(\pi_{T_i})=n_{T_i}$; fix one such prime for
0093: each support that occurs.
0094: 
0095: The supports $T_i$ cover $\mathcal P(n)$ because $H(q)$ is nonempty for every
0096: $q\in Q$. Moreover, $i$ belongs to $T_i$ and to no $T_j$ with $j\ne i$.
0097: Each $\pi_{T_i}$ is a prime jump, so
0098: $E_n(\pi_{T_i})=T_n(\pi_{T_i})=T_i$. Thus
0099: $\{\pi_{T_i}:i\in P\}$ is an $n$-witness cover. Distinct supports have
0100: distinct ranks and therefore distinct underlying primes. If two maps $H$
0101: differ, then their support families differ, since the edge containing the
0102: private coordinate $i$ identifies $T_i$; unique factorization then gives
0103: different minimal generators. There are
0104: $(2^r-1)^{\#Q}=(2^r-1)^{k-r}$ maps $H$, proving the lower bound in
0105: \eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}.
0106: 
0107: For the upper bound, let $\Theta$ be an $n$-witness cover with $s$ rank-jump factors. For
0108: each $\theta\in\Theta$, choose the least coordinate
0109: \[
0110:  x_\theta\in E_n(\theta)\setminus
0111:  \bigcup_{\eta\in\Theta\setminus\{\theta\}}T_n(\eta).
0112: \]
0113: These private coordinates are distinct; write
0114: $P=\{x_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ and
0115: $Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. If $x_\theta=x$, then
0116: \[
0117:  T_n(\theta)=\{x\}\cup U_\theta,\qquad U_\theta\subseteq Q,
0118: \]
0119: because every other member of $P$ is private to another rank-jump factor. By the
0120: prime--ladder alternative in Lemma~\ref{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}, either
0121: $E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta)$ or $E_n(\theta)=\{x\}$. Hence there are at most two
0122: support-pair alternatives, and the definition
0123: \eqref{eq:rank-window-multiplicity} allows at most $R(n)$ rank-jump factors for each.
0124: Thus, once $P$ is fixed, the rank-jump factor indexed by each
0125: $x\in P$ has at most $2R(n)2^{k-s}$ choices. Ignoring coverage and
0126: coprimeness only enlarges the count, so summing over the
0127: $\binom{k}{s}$ possible sets $P$ and over $1\le s\le k$ proves the upper
0128: bound in \eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}.
0129: 
0130: Now $r(k-r)=\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor$ and
0131: $(k-r)\log(1-2^{-r})=O(1)$. Hence the logarithm of the lower bound is
0132: $(\log2)k^2/4+O(1)$. For the upper bound, use
0133: $s(k-s)\le k^2/4$, $s\le k$, and
0134: $\sum_s\binom{k}{s}\le2^k$ to obtain
0135: \[
0136:  \log\sum_{s=1}^{k}\binom{k}{s}(2R(n))^s2^{s(k-s)}
0137:  \le\frac{\log2}{4}k^2+k\log R(n)+O(k).
0138: \]
0139: This proves \eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}.
0140: 
0141: Let
0142: \[
0143:  \mathcal Q_n=\{p^e:p\mid F_n,\ 1\le e\le\nu_p(F_n)\}.
0144: \]
0145: This set has cardinality $\Omega(F_n)$.  By unique factorization, the map
0146: \[
0147:  m\longmapsto\{p^{\nu_p(m)}:p\mid m\}
0148: \]
0149: is injective from $\mathcal M_n$ into the subsets of $\mathcal Q_n$.
0150: Corollary~\ref{cor:support-bound} says that every image has at most
0151: $k=\omega(n)$ members.  This proves the first inequality in
0152: \eqref{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}.
0153: 
0154: Since every prime factor of $F_n$ is at least $2$,
0155: $2^{\Omega(F_n)}\le F_n$.  Also $F_n<2^{n-1}$ for $n\ge3$, by the elementary
0156: induction $F_{j+1}=F_j+F_{j-1}<2^j$.  Hence
0157: $\Omega(F_n)\le n-2$.  A subset of an $N$-element set having at most $k$
0158: members can be encoded injectively by its increasing list padded to length
0159: $k$ with a new symbol; therefore
0160: \[
0161:  \sum_{r=0}^k\binom Nr\le(N+1)^k.
0162: \]
0163: Taking $N=\Omega(F_n)$ gives the second inequality in
0164: \eqref{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}.
0165: 
0166: The classical maximal-order formula for $\omega(n)$
0167: \cite[Theorem~22.11]{HardyWright2008Introduction}
0168: \[
0169:  \limsup_{n\to\infty}
0170:  \frac{\omega(n)\log\log n}{\log n}=1
0171: \]
0172: now combines with $L(n)\le\omega(n)\log n$ to prove
0173: \eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order}. This argument uses only the crude estimate
0174: $\#\mathcal M_n\le n^{\omega(n)}$, not the witness-cover entropy bound. On
0175: the other hand,
0176: $\mathcal M_n$ is an antichain in the divisor lattice of $F_n$, so
0177: \[
0178:  \#\mathcal M_n\le\widthop(\operatorname{Div}(F_n))\le\tau(F_n).
0179: \]
0180: Wigert's maximal-order theorem \cite{Wigert1907Divisors} states that
0181: \[
0182:  \log\tau(N)\le(\log2+o(1))\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.
0183: \]
0184: Binet's formula gives $\log F_n=n\log\varphi+O(1)$ and
0185: $\log\log F_n=\log n+O(1)$, yielding
0186: \eqref{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}.  Finally,
0187: $(\log n)^2/\log\log n=o(n/\log n)$, so
0188: \eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order} gives the stated strict improvement.
0189: 
0190: For the mean upper bound, use the classical mean-value estimate
0191: \cite{HardyRamanujan1917NormalPrimeFactors}
0192: \begin{equation}
0193: \label{eq:mean-omega-input}
0194:  \sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+O(x),
0195: \end{equation}
0196: together with $L(n)\le\omega(n)\log n$.  Uniformly for $n\le x$,
0197: $\log n\le\log x$, and hence
0198: \[
0199:  \sum_{3\le n\le x}L(n)
0200:  \le\log x\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)
0201:  =(1+o(1))x\log x\,\log\log x.
0202: \]
0203: 
0204: Tur\'an's second-moment form of the Hardy--Ramanujan theorem
0205: \cite{Turan1934HardyRamanujan} gives
0206: \begin{equation}\label{eq:omega-second-moment}
0207:  \sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)^2=(1+o(1))x(\log\log x)^2.
0208: \end{equation}
0209: After enlarging the absolute constant in the lower half of
0210: \eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}, it holds as
0211: $L(n)\ge(\log2)\omega(n)^2/4-O(1)$ also for $\omega(n)<3$.
0212: Summation and \eqref{eq:omega-second-moment} prove the lower half of
0213: \eqref{eq:mean-logarithmic-growth} and complete the proof.
0214: \end{proof}
0215:
