-\subsection{Exact-rank primes and primitive divisors}\label{subsec:primitive}
-
-A prime $p$ is an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} if $\alpha(p)=d$;
-when it is viewed as a rank-jump prime power, we also call it a \emph{prime
-jump}. We reserve \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} for the standard
-Carmichael--Bilu--Hanrot--Voutier convention: a prime $p$ dividing $F_d$ is
-primitive when
-\[
- p\nmid 5F_1F_2\cdots F_{d-1}.
-\]
-Thus every primitive divisor is an exact-rank prime, but the exact-rank prime
-$5$ at rank $5$ is excluded from the primitive-divisor terminology because it
-divides the discriminant. This distinction will be maintained throughout.
-
-\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
-For every $n\ge 3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there exists a prime $p_n$ with
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For $n=3,4,5$ one takes $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$; the last is the
-discriminant-related exact-rank exception just described. For $n\ge 7$,
-$n\neq 12$, the primitive divisor theorem
-\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,Yabuta2001PrimitiveDivisorFibonacci,%
-BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}
-gives a prime dividing $F_n$ but no earlier Fibonacci number. Since
-$\alpha(p_n)\mid n$ and $p_n$ divides no $F_d$ with $d<n$, necessarily
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Counting corollaries}\label{subsec:counting}
-
-The standard M\"obius-inversion formulas for first-appearance counts follow
-from Stroi\'nski's $\alpha$-contraction identity
-\cite{Stroinski2016AlphaContraction}: for any $f:\NN\to\mathbb{C}$ with
-$f(1)=0$,
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stroinski}
-\sum_{d\mid F_n}f(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}f_\alpha(d),
-\qquad
-f_\alpha(d):=\sum_{\alpha(m)=d}f(m).
-\end{equation}
-Taking $f$ to be the indicator of integers at least $2$, of primes, or of
-prime powers, and applying M\"obius inversion, one obtains
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:mobius-birth}
-A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\tau(F_d),
-\qquad
-A_{\mathrm{pr}}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\omega(F_d).
-\end{equation}
-We regard these as known corollaries; the witness-cover classification below
-is independent of them.
-
-\begin{lemma}[Exact-rank prime M\"obius count]\label{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}
-For $d\ge1$, put
-\[
-\Pi_\alpha(d):=\{p\text{ prime}:\alpha(p)=d\}.
-\]
-Then $\Pi_\alpha(d)$ is finite and
-\[
-\#\Pi_\alpha(d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\mu(d/c)\,\omega(F_c).
-\]
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For each $d\ge1$, the primes with rank dividing $d$ are exactly the prime
-divisors of $F_d$: indeed, for a prime $p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}
-gives $p\mid F_d$ if and only if $\alpha(p)\mid d$.  Hence
-Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} partitions the distinct prime divisors of
-$F_d$ according to their exact ranks $c\mid d$, including the exceptional
-primes $2$ and $5$ with ranks $3$ and $5$ respectively; a prime divisor of
-$F_c$ can occur earlier only through the condition $\alpha(p)\mid e$ for the
-earlier index $e$.
-\[
-\omega(F_d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\#\Pi_\alpha(c).
-\]
-The right-hand side is finite because $F_d$ has only finitely many prime
-divisors.  Applying M\"obius inversion on the divisor lattice of $d$ gives the
-displayed formula.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Rank-jump notation}\label{subsec:prime-power}
-
-\begin{definition}\label{def:rank-jump-families}
-For a prime power $\theta=p^e$ with $e\ge1$, put
-\[
-d(\theta):=\alpha(\theta),\qquad
-d^-(\theta):=\alpha(p^{e-1}),
-\]
-where $\alpha(1)=1$. For $d\ge1$ define
-\[
-\Atom(d):=\{p^e:\ \alpha(p^e)=d,\ \alpha(p^{e-1})<d\}.
-\]
-Thus $\Atom(d)$ consists of the prime-power factors at which the rank first
-jumps to $d$ when the exponent is increased.
-
-If $d(\theta)\mid n$, define the full-coordinate support and the
-essential-coordinate support of $\theta$ relative to $n$ by
-\[
-T_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\
-\nu_\ell(d(\theta))=\nu_\ell(n)\},
-\]
-and
-\[
-E_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in T_n(\theta):\
-\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta))<\nu_\ell(n)\}.
-\]
-Equivalently, $T_n(\theta)$ records the prime coordinates of $n$ supplied at
-full exponent by $d(\theta)$, while $E_n(\theta)$ records the full coordinates

+The finiteness of $\alpha(q)$ follows from the periodicity of the Fibonacci
+state vector modulo $q$; see, for example, Wall
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm}. We use the following standard facts.
+
+\begin{proposition}\label{prop:rank-basics}
+For positive integers $q,u,v,a,b,m$,
+\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
+\item $q\mid F_m$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$;
+\item $\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$;
+\item $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))=\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$.
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The first two statements are classical
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm,Vinson1963RankApparition}. For the last, an integer
+$m$ is divisible by $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ exactly when both $u$ and $v$
+divide $F_m$, hence exactly when both $\alpha(u)$ and $\alpha(v)$ divide $m$.
+The two sides therefore have the same positive multiples. This lcm identity
+also appears in \cite{LucaTron2015SelfFibonacciDivisors,Renault2013PeriodRankOrder}.
+\end{proof}
+
+We call $p$ an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} when $\alpha(p)=d$.
+The term \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} retains its standard meaning: a
+prime dividing $F_d$ but not $5F_1\cdots F_{d-1}$. Thus the exact-rank prime
+$5$ at rank $5$ is not primitive in this terminology.
+
+\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]
+\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
+For every $n\geq3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there is a prime $p_n$ such that
+$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Take $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$. For $n\geq7$, $n\ne12$, the primitive
+divisor theorem
+\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,Yabuta2001PrimitiveDivisorFibonacci,%
+BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}
+supplies a prime dividing $F_n$ and no earlier Fibonacci number, so its rank
+is $n$.
+\end{proof}

+\section{Quantitative bounds}\label{sec:growth}
+
+For $n\geq3$, define the rank-window multiplicity precisely by
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-window-multiplicity}
+ R(n):=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}
+ \#\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)\right\}.
+\end{equation}
+Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots} shows that this number is
+finite: prime-jump families are finite unions of exact-rank prime classes,
+and each ladder family contains at most one factor.
+
+\begin{lemma}[Deaggregation of a rank window]
+\label{lem:rank-window-deaggregation}
+For $d\mid n$, put
+\[
+ T_n(d)=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}
+\]
+and
+\[
+ A^*(n)=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)\ne\varnothing}}a(d)\right\}.
+\]
+If $n=\prod_\ell\ell^{e_\ell}$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}
+ 0\leq\log R(n)-\log A^*(n)
+ \leq\log2+\sum_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}\log e_\ell.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, let
+\[
+ W_J(n)=\{d\mid n:T_n(d)=J\}.
+\]
+Then $\#W_J(n)=\prod_{\ell\notin J}e_\ell$, and the prime jumps with
+$(E_n,T_n)=(J,J)$ form the disjoint union of the classes
+$\Pi_\alpha(d)$ for $d\in W_J(n)$. All other nonempty families are ladder
+families of size at most one. Hence, with
+\[
+ P(n)=\max_{J\ne\varnothing}\sum_{d\in W_J(n)}a(d),
+\]
+we have $P(n)\leq R(n)\leq P(n)+1$. It follows that
+\[
+ A^*(n)\leq R(n)
+ \leq1+A^*(n)\prod_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}e_\ell,
+\]
+which gives \eqref{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal-generator-growth}]
+For $n\geq3$, the strict increase of the Fibonacci sequence from index $2$
+onward gives $\alpha(F_n)=n$. Thus $B_n$ is a nonempty finite poset and
+$\mathcal M_n\ne\varnothing$.
+
+Assume $k\geq3$, order $\mathcal P(n)$, and put $r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$.
+Choose an $r$-set
+$P\subseteq\mathcal P(n)\setminus\{2,3\}$ and put
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. For each map
+\[
+ H:Q\longrightarrow2^P\setminus\{\varnothing\}
+\]
+and $i\in P$, define
+\[
+ T_i=\{i\}\cup\{q\in Q:i\in H(q)\}.
+\]
+The integer $n_{T_i}$ has a prime divisor outside $\{2,3\}$, so it is not
+$6$ or $12$. Choose an exact-rank prime $\pi_{T_i}$ of rank $n_{T_i}$ by
+Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors}. The supports $T_i$ cover
+$\mathcal P(n)$, and $i$ is private to $T_i$; hence the primes $\pi_{T_i}$
+form a witness cover. Different maps give different support families and,
+by unique factorization, different elements of $\mathcal M_n$. There are
+$(2^r-1)^{k-r}$ such maps, proving the lower bound.
+
+For the upper bound, let $\Theta$ be a witness cover with $s$ factors. Choose
+the least private coordinate $x_\theta$ of each $\theta\in\Theta$. These
+coordinates are distinct; write $P=\{x_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ and
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. If $x_\theta=x$, then
+\[
+ T_n(\theta)=\{x\}\cup U_\theta,\qquad U_\theta\subseteq Q.
+\]
+By Lemma~\ref{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}, either
+$E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta)$ or $E_n(\theta)=\{x\}$. For fixed $x$ this gives
+at most $2R(n)2^{k-s}$ choices. Ignoring coverage and coprimeness only
+increases the count, so summing over the $\binom{k}{s}$ possible private sets
+and $1\leq s\leq k$ proves the upper bound in
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}.
+
+Finally, $r(k-r)=\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor$ and
+$(k-r)\log(1-2^{-r})=O(1)$. For the upper bound use
+$s(k-s)\leq k^2/4$, $s\leq k$, and
+$\sum_s\binom{k}{s}\leq2^k$. Taking logarithms gives
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}.
+\end{proof}
+
+The term $\omega(n)\log R(n)$ depends on the multiplicities $a(d)$ of
+individual exact ranks, as Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-window-deaggregation} makes
+explicit. Presently available existence and cumulative primitive-divisor
+estimates do not remove this term. Consequently
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order} does not give an unconditional
+almost-all equivalent for $\log\#\mathcal M_n$; such a result would also have
+to control witness covers outside the rank-pure sector.

+\section{Secondary counting bounds}

+\begin{corollary}[Coarse and mean bounds]\label{cor:secondary-bounds}
+For $n\geq3$, put $k=\omega(n)$ and $L(n)=\log\#\mathcal M_n$. Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}
+ \#\mathcal M_n
+ \leq\sum_{r=0}^k\binom{\Omega(F_n)}r
+ \leq n^k,
+\end{equation}
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:crude-maximal-order}
+ \limsup_{n\to\infty}
+ \frac{L(n)\log\log n}{(\log n)^2}\leq1,
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2\,\log\varphi+o(1))\frac n{\log n},
+ \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
+\end{equation}
+Moreover, as $x\to\infty$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:mean-logarithmic-growth}
+ \left(\frac{\log2}{4}+o(1)\right)x(\log\log x)^2
+ \leq\sum_{3\leq n\leq x}L(n)
+ \leq(1+o(1))x\log x\,\log\log x.
+\end{equation}
+\end{corollary}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Unique factorization injects $\mathcal M_n$ into the subsets of the
+$\Omega(F_n)$ prime powers dividing $F_n$. Theorem~
+\ref{article-thm:witness-classification} bounds the subset size by $k$,
+giving the first inequality in \eqref{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}.
+Since $2^{\Omega(F_n)}\leq F_n<2^{n-1}$, we have
+$\Omega(F_n)\leq n-2$, and
+$\sum_{r=0}^k\binom Nr\leq(N+1)^k$ gives the second.
+
+The classical maximal order of $\omega(n)$
+\cite[Theorem~22.11]{HardyWright2008Introduction} applied to
+$L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$ proves
+\eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order}. Since $\mathcal M_n$ is an antichain in the
+divisor lattice of $F_n$, Wigert's theorem \cite{Wigert1907Divisors} gives
+\[
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2+o(1))\frac{\log F_n}{\log\log F_n}.
+\]
+Binet's formula yields \eqref{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}.
+
+For the mean upper bound, use
+\cite{HardyRamanujan1917NormalPrimeFactors} in the form
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+O(x)
+\]
+and $L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$. For the lower bound, Tur\'an's second-moment
+form of the Hardy--Ramanujan theorem \cite{Turan1934HardyRamanujan} gives
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)^2=(1+o(1))x(\log\log x)^2.
+\]
+The lower half of \eqref{article-eq:private-cover-entropy-order}, after
+enlarging its absolute constant for $\omega(n)<3$, completes the proof.
+\end{proof}
+
+For a labelled $k$-set $V$, let $C_k$ be the number of irredundant covers of
+$V$ by nonempty subsets.
+
+\begin{proposition}[Sharp cumulative-data bound]
+\label{prop:sharp-cumulative-data-obstruction}
+Assign a real weight $w_S\geq1$ to every nonempty $S\subseteq V$, and put
+\[
+ Z_V(w)=\sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
+              \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}w_S,
+ \qquad A=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}w_S.
+\]
+Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}
+ Z_V(w)\geq C_k+A-(2^k-1).
+\end{equation}
+This is best possible for every $A\geq2^k-1$: equality is attained by
+\[
+ w_V=A-(2^k-2),\qquad w_S=1\quad(S\ne V).
+\]
+If $k\geq3$, this is the only equality profile.
+
+Consequently, if $n\geq3$ is odd and squarefree and $k=\omega(n)$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-rank-pure-bound}
+ \#\{m\in\mathcal M_n:\mu^2(m)=1\}
+ \geq C_k+\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1),
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-weighted-excess}
+ \mathcal W(n)\geq
+ 1+\frac{\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1)}{C_k}.
+\end{equation}
+Among positive weight profiles with the same total
+$\sum_{d\mid n,\ d>1}a(d)=\omega(F_n)$, this conclusion is exact. The
+extremizing profile is not asserted to occur among Fibonacci exact-rank
+multiplicities.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Write $w_S=1+x_S$ with $x_S\geq0$. For every minimal cover $\mathcal C$,
+\[
+ \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}(1+x_S)
+ \geq1+\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}x_S.
+\]
+Every nonempty $S\subseteq V$ occurs in a minimal cover: use $\{V\}$ for
+$S=V$, and otherwise use
+$\{S\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V\setminus S\}$. Summation proves
+\eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}. The only minimal cover containing
+$V$ is $\{V\}$, so the displayed profile attains equality.
+
+If $k\geq3$, every proper nonempty $S$ occurs in at least two minimal covers.
+For $|S|=1$, use the singleton partition and $\{S,V\setminus S\}$; for
+$|S|\geq2$, choose $s\in S$, $t\notin S$, and also use the cover consisting
+of $S$, $\{s,t\}$, and the remaining singletons. Equality therefore forces
+$x_S=0$ for every proper $S$.
+
+For odd squarefree $n$, nonempty subsets of $\mathcal P(n)$ correspond to
+divisors $d>1$ of $n$, and exact ranks partition the prime divisors of $F_n$:
+\[
+ \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}a(n_S)=\omega(F_n).
+\]
+Apply \eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}, Theorem~
+\ref{article-cor:canonical-squarefree-slice}, and
+\eqref{article-eq:weighted-cover-excess}.
+\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
-For every $n\ge2$,
-\[
-B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.
-\]
-Moreover $B_n$ is an upper set in $D_n$: if $q\in B_n$, $r\in D_n$, and

-\[
-B_n=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M_n}\{q\in D_n:\ m\mid q\}.

-\begin{proof}
-By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}, an integer $q$ lies in $D_m$ if and
-only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$. Thus $q\in D_n$ lies outside
-$\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}$ precisely when $\alpha(q)\mid n$ but

-If $\alpha(q)=n$, then clearly $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every $p\mid n$, so
-$q$ is outside the union. Conversely, suppose $\alpha(q)\mid n$ and

-$F_{\alpha(r)}$ gives $\alpha(q)\mid\alpha(r)$. But $\alpha(q)=n$, so
-$n\mid\alpha(r)$ and $\alpha(r)\mid n$, whence $\alpha(r)=n$. Therefore
-$r\in B_n$.

-Finally $D_n$ is finite, so every element $q\in B_n$ has at least one

-some $m\in\mathcal M_n$ lies again in $B_n$. This proves the displayed

-\begin{lemma}[Minimal-lcm criterion]\label{thm:minimal-generators}
-Let $n\ge2$, and let
-$m=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ be a divisor of $F_n$, with the $p_i$ distinct

-\[

-\]

-\begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm-criterion}

-\quad\text{and}\quad
-\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,

-\quad(1\le i\le r).
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}

-\begin{proof}
-Because $m\mid F_n$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives
-$\lambda_i\mid n$ for every $i$. Applying the lcm identity in

-\[
-\alpha(m)=\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r).

-Thus the first condition in \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion} is equivalent to

-still a divisor of $F_n$. Minimality of $m$ in $B_n$ implies

-\[

+Let $D_n=\operatorname{Div}(F_n)$. The exact rank fiber can be read directly
+inside this divisor lattice.

+\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
+For every $n\geq2$,
+\[
+ B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.
+\]
+Moreover, $B_n$ is an upper set in $D_n$, and hence
+\[
+ B_n=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M_n}\{q\in D_n:m\mid q\}.
+\]
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}, $q\in D_n$ lies outside every
+$D_{n/p}$ precisely when $\alpha(q)\mid n$ but $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for each
+prime $p\mid n$, which is equivalent to $\alpha(q)=n$. If $q\mid r\mid F_n$
+and $\alpha(q)=n$, then $n=\alpha(q)\mid\alpha(r)\mid n$, so $r\in B_n$.
+The final identity follows by taking minimal elements in the finite upper set.
 \end{proof}
 
-\subsection*{Witness covers}
-
-\begin{definition}\label{def:witness-cover}
-An \emph{$n$-witness cover} is a finite set
-$\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ of rank-jump prime powers satisfying:
-\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
-\item $d(\theta)\mid n$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$;
-\item the elements of $\Theta$ are pairwise coprime;
-\item the full-coordinate supports cover all prime coordinates of $n$,
-\[
-\bigcup_{\theta\in\Theta}T_n(\theta)=\mathcal P(n);
-\]
-\item each rank-jump factor has an essential coordinate not supplied by the other rank-jump factors,
-\[
-E_n(\theta)\nsubseteq
-\bigcup_{\eta\in\Theta,\ \eta\ne\theta}T_n(\eta)
-\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).
-\]
-\end{enumerate}
-The last condition is the irredundance condition. It is stated with
-$E_n$ rather than $T_n$ because overlapping full-coordinate support is
-allowed; what is forbidden is that every coordinate lost by lowering
-$\theta$ is already supplied at full exponent by the remaining rank-jump factors.
-\end{definition}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Coordinate test for lowering one rank-jump factor]
-\label{lem:coordinate-lowering-test}
-Let $n\ge2$, and let
-$\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ be a pairwise coprime set of rank-jump
-prime powers with $d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and
-\[
-\lcmop(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r))=n.
-\]
-Fix $\theta_i=p_i^{e_i}$, and put
-\[
-N_i^-:=\lcmop\bigl(d^-(\theta_i),\ d(\theta_j):j\ne i\bigr).
-\]
-Then $N_i^-=n$ if and only if
-\[
-E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j).
-\]
-Equivalently, lowering $\theta_i$ to $p_i^{e_i-1}$ keeps the apparition lcm
-equal to $n$ exactly when every coordinate lost by the lowering is supplied at
-full exponent by some other rank-jump factor. If
-$\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, then
-$\nu_\ell(N_i^-)<\nu_\ell(n)$, so $N_i^-<n$.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Since $d^-(\theta_i)\mid d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and $d(\theta_j)\mid n$ for
-$j\ne i$, the integer $N_i^-$ divides $n$. Hence $N_i^-=n$ is equivalent to
-saying that every prime coordinate $\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$ occurs in $N_i^-$
-with valuation $\nu_\ell(n)$.
-
-Assume first that
-$E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, and fix
-$\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$. Because the original lcm is $n$, at least one of the
-numbers $d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r)$ supplies the full
-$\ell$-adic valuation of $n$. If such a supplier is some $d(\theta_j)$ with
-$j\ne i$, then $\ell\in T_n(\theta_j)$ and the same full valuation appears in
-$N_i^-$. The only remaining case is that $\theta_i$ itself supplies the full
-valuation and no other rank-jump factor does, so $\ell\in T_n(\theta_i)$ and
-$\ell\notin\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The assumed containment then gives
-$\ell\notin E_n(\theta_i)$. By the definition of $E_n(\theta_i)$,
-$\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))=\nu_\ell(n)$, so the lowered factor still supplies the
-full $\ell$-coordinate in $N_i^-$. Thus every coordinate of $n$ is still
-present at full valuation, and $N_i^-=n$.
-
-Conversely, suppose that some coordinate
-$\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ is not in $\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The
-membership $\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ says
-$\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))<\nu_\ell(n)$. For every $j\ne i$, the exclusion
-$\ell\notin T_n(\theta_j)$ says
-$\nu_\ell(d(\theta_j))<\nu_\ell(n)$. Therefore the lcm defining $N_i^-$ also
-has $\ell$-adic valuation strictly below $\nu_\ell(n)$. Since $N_i^-\mid n$,
-this proves $N_i^-<n$.
+\begin{lemma}[Minimal-lcm criterion]\label{thm:minimal-generators}
+Let $n\geq2$, and let $m=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ divide $F_n$, with the
+$p_i$ distinct. Put
+\[
+ \lambda_i=\alpha(p_i^{e_i}),\qquad
+ \lambda_i^-=\alpha(p_i^{e_i-1}).
+\]
+Then $m\in\mathcal M_n$ if and only if
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm-criterion}
+ \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)=n
+\end{equation}
+and, for every $i$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:lowered-lcm-criterion}
+ \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,
+        \lambda_{i+1},\ldots,\lambda_r)<n.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Repeated use of Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives
+$\alpha(m)=\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)$ and replaces $\lambda_i$ by
+$\lambda_i^-$ for $m/p_i$. Thus minimality implies both displays. Conversely,
+if they hold and $q$ is a proper divisor of $m$, then for some $i$ the
+$p_i$-exponent of $q$ is at most $e_i-1$, so
+\[
+ \alpha(q)\mid\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_i^-,\ldots,\lambda_r)<n.
+\]
+Hence no proper divisor of $m$ belongs to $B_n$.
 \end{proof}

 \begin{proof}
-For a prime jump $p_i$, one has $d^-(p_i)=\alpha(1)=1$. Hence replacing

-For arbitrary rank-jump factors, the same two lemmas say exactly that the full apparition

+For a prime jump $p_i$, $d^-(p_i)=\alpha(1)=1$, so lowering its label is the
+same as deleting it. In general, the full supports cover $\mathcal P(n)$

+\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification}]
+Let $m\in\mathcal M_n$, and write
+$m=\prod_{i=1}^r\theta_i$ with $\theta_i=p_i^{e_i}$ and the $p_i$ distinct.

-\begin{theorem}\label{thm:witness-classification}
-For every $n\ge 2$, multiplication gives a bijection
-\[
-\Theta\longmapsto \prod_{\theta\in\Theta}\theta
-\]
-from the set of $n$-witness covers onto $\mathcal M_n$. Its inverse sends
-$m\in\mathcal M_n$ to the set
-\[
-\Theta(m):=\{p^{\nu_p(m)}:p\mid m\}
-\]
-of prime-power factors occurring in the prime factorization of $m$. In
-particular,
-\[
-\mathcal M_n=\bigl\{\prod_{\theta\in\Theta}\theta:
-\Theta\text{ is an $n$-witness cover}\bigr\},
-\]
-and each element of $\mathcal M_n$ has a unique witness-cover factorization.
-Here uniqueness is inherited from unique factorization in $\mathbb Z$; the
-substantive assertion is the witness-cover admissibility criterion.
-\end{theorem}

-\begin{proof}

-\end{proof}

-\subsection*{Organization}
+Wagner's minimal multiplicative covers
+\cite{Wagner1978MultiplicativeCovers} supply the classical prime-jump
+skeleton: deleting one lcm label must lower the lcm. Fibonacci prime-power
+lifting adds the predecessor $d^-(\theta)$, so a ladder label must be lowered
+rather than deleted. Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification} identifies
+exactly which such covers are the minimal rank fibers.

-\subsection{Rank of apparition and Fibonacci divisibility}\label{subsec:fib-div}

-\begin{lemma}[Finite rank of apparition]\label{lem:finite-rank}
-For every integer $q\ge1$, the rank of apparition $\alpha(q)$ is finite.  More
-precisely, $\alpha(1)=1$, and for every $q\ge2$ there is a positive integer
-$r$ such that $q\mid F_r$.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The case $q=1$ is the stated convention.  Let $q\ge2$.  Work modulo $q$ with
-the Fibonacci state vector $(F_m,F_{m+1})$.  The transition
-\[
-(x,y)\longmapsto (y,x+y)
-\]
-has inverse $(x,y)\mapsto (y-x,x)$ modulo $q$, so it is a permutation of the
-finite set $(\ZZ/q\ZZ)^2$.  Therefore the orbit of the initial state $(0,1)$
-is periodic and returns to $(0,1)$ after some positive number $r$ of steps.
-Thus $(F_r,F_{r+1})\equiv(0,1)\pmod q$, in particular $q\mid F_r$.  The
-least such positive $r$ exists by well ordering.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{proposition}\label{prop:rank-basics}
-Let $q,u,v\ge1$ and let $a,b,m\ge1$. Then:
-\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
-\item $q\mid F_m$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$.
-\item $\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$.
-\item $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))=\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$.
-\end{enumerate}
-\end{proposition}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The divisibility criterion and the strong-divisibility identity are classical;
-we use them in the forms proved by Wall \cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm} and
-Vinson \cite{Vinson1963RankApparition}. The convention $\alpha(1)=1$ makes
-the assertion for $q=1$ immediate.
+\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:prelim}
 
-The Fibonacci lcm identity is recorded by Luca--Tron
-\cite{LucaTron2015SelfFibonacciDivisors}; Renault gives the corresponding
-identity for the more general $(a,b)$-Fibonacci sequences
-\cite{Renault2013PeriodRankOrder}. For completeness, an integer $m$ is
-divisible by
-$\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ if and only if $\lcmop(u,v)\mid F_m$, by (i). This is
-equivalent to $u\mid F_m$ and $v\mid F_m$, hence to
-$\alpha(u)\mid m$ and $\alpha(v)\mid m$, again by (i). Thus the multiples of
-$\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ are exactly the multiples of
-$\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$, and the two positive integers are equal.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Exact-rank primes and primitive divisors}\label{subsec:primitive}
-
-A prime $p$ is an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} if $\alpha(p)=d$;
-when it is viewed as a rank-jump prime power, we also call it a \emph{prime
-jump}. We reserve \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} for the standard
-Carmichael--Bilu--Hanrot--Voutier convention: a prime $p$ dividing $F_d$ is
-primitive when
-\[
- p\nmid 5F_1F_2\cdots F_{d-1}.
-\]
-Thus every primitive divisor is an exact-rank prime, but the exact-rank prime
-$5$ at rank $5$ is excluded from the primitive-divisor terminology because it
-divides the discriminant. This distinction will be maintained throughout.
-
-\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
-For every $n\ge 3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there exists a prime $p_n$ with
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For $n=3,4,5$ one takes $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$; the last is the
-discriminant-related exact-rank exception just described. For $n\ge 7$,
-$n\neq 12$, the primitive divisor theorem
-\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,Yabuta2001PrimitiveDivisorFibonacci,%
-BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}
-gives a prime dividing $F_n$ but no earlier Fibonacci number. Since
-$\alpha(p_n)\mid n$ and $p_n$ divides no $F_d$ with $d<n$, necessarily
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Counting corollaries}\label{subsec:counting}
-
-The standard M\"obius-inversion formulas for first-appearance counts follow
-from Stroi\'nski's $\alpha$-contraction identity
-\cite{Stroinski2016AlphaContraction}: for any $f:\NN\to\mathbb{C}$ with
-$f(1)=0$,
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stroinski}
-\sum_{d\mid F_n}f(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}f_\alpha(d),
-\qquad
-f_\alpha(d):=\sum_{\alpha(m)=d}f(m).
-\end{equation}
-Taking $f$ to be the indicator of integers at least $2$, of primes, or of
-prime powers, and applying M\"obius inversion, one obtains
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:mobius-birth}
-A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\tau(F_d),
-\qquad
-A_{\mathrm{pr}}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\omega(F_d).
-\end{equation}
-We regard these as known corollaries; the witness-cover classification below
-is independent of them.

-\begin{lemma}[Exact-rank prime M\"obius count]\label{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}
-For $d\ge1$, put
-\[
-\Pi_\alpha(d):=\{p\text{ prime}:\alpha(p)=d\}.
-\]
-Then $\Pi_\alpha(d)$ is finite and
-\[
-\#\Pi_\alpha(d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\mu(d/c)\,\omega(F_c).
-\]
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For each $d\ge1$, the primes with rank dividing $d$ are exactly the prime
-divisors of $F_d$: indeed, for a prime $p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}
-gives $p\mid F_d$ if and only if $\alpha(p)\mid d$.  Hence
-Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} partitions the distinct prime divisors of
-$F_d$ according to their exact ranks $c\mid d$, including the exceptional
-primes $2$ and $5$ with ranks $3$ and $5$ respectively; a prime divisor of
-$F_c$ can occur earlier only through the condition $\alpha(p)\mid e$ for the
-earlier index $e$.
-\[
-\omega(F_d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\#\Pi_\alpha(c).
-\]
-The right-hand side is finite because $F_d$ has only finitely many prime
-divisors.  Applying M\"obius inversion on the divisor lattice of $d$ gives the
-displayed formula.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Rank-jump notation}\label{subsec:prime-power}
-
-\begin{definition}\label{def:rank-jump-families}
-For a prime power $\theta=p^e$ with $e\ge1$, put
-\[
-d(\theta):=\alpha(\theta),\qquad
-d^-(\theta):=\alpha(p^{e-1}),
-\]
-where $\alpha(1)=1$. For $d\ge1$ define
-\[
-\Atom(d):=\{p^e:\ \alpha(p^e)=d,\ \alpha(p^{e-1})<d\}.
-\]
-Thus $\Atom(d)$ consists of the prime-power factors at which the rank first
-jumps to $d$ when the exponent is increased.
-
-If $d(\theta)\mid n$, define the full-coordinate support and the
-essential-coordinate support of $\theta$ relative to $n$ by
-\[
-T_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\
-\nu_\ell(d(\theta))=\nu_\ell(n)\},
-\]
-and
-\[
-E_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in T_n(\theta):\
-\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta))<\nu_\ell(n)\}.
-\]
-Equivalently, $T_n(\theta)$ records the prime coordinates of $n$ supplied at
-full exponent by $d(\theta)$, while $E_n(\theta)$ records the full coordinates
-lost when $\theta=p^e$ is lowered to $p^{e-1}$.
-
-For nonempty $I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, put
-\[
-\mathcal A_{I,J}(n):=
-\{\theta\in\bigcup_{d\mid n}\Atom(d):\
-E_n(\theta)=I,\ T_n(\theta)=J\}.
-\]
-\end{definition}
+The finiteness of $\alpha(q)$ follows from the periodicity of the Fibonacci
+state vector modulo $q$; see, for example, Wall
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm}. We use the following standard facts.
+
+\begin{proposition}\label{prop:rank-basics}
+For positive integers $q,u,v,a,b,m$,
+\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
+\item $q\mid F_m$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$;
+\item $\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$;
+\item $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))=\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$.
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The first two statements are classical
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm,Vinson1963RankApparition}. For the last, an integer
+$m$ is divisible by $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ exactly when both $u$ and $v$
+divide $F_m$, hence exactly when both $\alpha(u)$ and $\alpha(v)$ divide $m$.
+The two sides therefore have the same positive multiples. This lcm identity
+also appears in \cite{LucaTron2015SelfFibonacciDivisors,Renault2013PeriodRankOrder}.
+\end{proof}
+
+We call $p$ an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} when $\alpha(p)=d$.
+The term \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} retains its standard meaning: a
+prime dividing $F_d$ but not $5F_1\cdots F_{d-1}$. Thus the exact-rank prime
+$5$ at rank $5$ is not primitive in this terminology.
+
+\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]
+\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
+For every $n\geq3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there is a prime $p_n$ such that
+$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Take $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$. For $n\geq7$, $n\ne12$, the primitive
+divisor theorem
+\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,Yabuta2001PrimitiveDivisorFibonacci,%
+BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}
+supplies a prime dividing $F_n$ and no earlier Fibonacci number, so its rank
+is $n$.
+\end{proof}

+\section{Quantitative bounds}\label{sec:growth}
+
+For $n\geq3$, define the rank-window multiplicity precisely by
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-window-multiplicity}
+ R(n):=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}
+ \#\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)\right\}.
+\end{equation}
+Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots} shows that this number is
+finite: prime-jump families are finite unions of exact-rank prime classes,
+and each ladder family contains at most one factor.
+
+\begin{lemma}[Deaggregation of a rank window]
+\label{lem:rank-window-deaggregation}
+For $d\mid n$, put
+\[
+ T_n(d)=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}
+\]
+and
+\[
+ A^*(n)=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)\ne\varnothing}}a(d)\right\}.
+\]
+If $n=\prod_\ell\ell^{e_\ell}$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}
+ 0\leq\log R(n)-\log A^*(n)
+ \leq\log2+\sum_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}\log e_\ell.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, let
+\[
+ W_J(n)=\{d\mid n:T_n(d)=J\}.
+\]
+Then $\#W_J(n)=\prod_{\ell\notin J}e_\ell$, and the prime jumps with
+$(E_n,T_n)=(J,J)$ form the disjoint union of the classes
+$\Pi_\alpha(d)$ for $d\in W_J(n)$. All other nonempty families are ladder
+families of size at most one. Hence, with
+\[
+ P(n)=\max_{J\ne\varnothing}\sum_{d\in W_J(n)}a(d),
+\]
+we have $P(n)\leq R(n)\leq P(n)+1$. It follows that
+\[
+ A^*(n)\leq R(n)
+ \leq1+A^*(n)\prod_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}e_\ell,
+\]
+which gives \eqref{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal-generator-growth}]
+For $n\geq3$, the strict increase of the Fibonacci sequence from index $2$
+onward gives $\alpha(F_n)=n$. Thus $B_n$ is a nonempty finite poset and
+$\mathcal M_n\ne\varnothing$.
+
+Assume $k\geq3$, order $\mathcal P(n)$, and put $r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$.
+Choose an $r$-set
+$P\subseteq\mathcal P(n)\setminus\{2,3\}$ and put
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. For each map
+\[
+ H:Q\longrightarrow2^P\setminus\{\varnothing\}
+\]
+and $i\in P$, define
+\[
+ T_i=\{i\}\cup\{q\in Q:i\in H(q)\}.
+\]
+The integer $n_{T_i}$ has a prime divisor outside $\{2,3\}$, so it is not
+$6$ or $12$. Choose an exact-rank prime $\pi_{T_i}$ of rank $n_{T_i}$ by
+Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors}. The supports $T_i$ cover
+$\mathcal P(n)$, and $i$ is private to $T_i$; hence the primes $\pi_{T_i}$
+form a witness cover. Different maps give different support families and,
+by unique factorization, different elements of $\mathcal M_n$. There are
+$(2^r-1)^{k-r}$ such maps, proving the lower bound.
+
+For the upper bound, let $\Theta$ be a witness cover with $s$ factors. Choose
+the least private coordinate $x_\theta$ of each $\theta\in\Theta$. These
+coordinates are distinct; write $P=\{x_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ and
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. If $x_\theta=x$, then
+\[
+ T_n(\theta)=\{x\}\cup U_\theta,\qquad U_\theta\subseteq Q.
+\]
+By Lemma~\ref{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}, either
+$E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta)$ or $E_n(\theta)=\{x\}$. For fixed $x$ this gives
+at most $2R(n)2^{k-s}$ choices. Ignoring coverage and coprimeness only
+increases the count, so summing over the $\binom{k}{s}$ possible private sets
+and $1\leq s\leq k$ proves the upper bound in
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}.
+
+Finally, $r(k-r)=\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor$ and
+$(k-r)\log(1-2^{-r})=O(1)$. For the upper bound use
+$s(k-s)\leq k^2/4$, $s\leq k$, and
+$\sum_s\binom{k}{s}\leq2^k$. Taking logarithms gives
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}.
+\end{proof}
+
+The term $\omega(n)\log R(n)$ depends on the multiplicities $a(d)$ of
+individual exact ranks, as Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-window-deaggregation} makes
+explicit. Presently available existence and cumulative primitive-divisor
+estimates do not remove this term. Consequently
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order} does not give an unconditional
+almost-all equivalent for $\log\#\mathcal M_n$; such a result would also have
+to control witness covers outside the rank-pure sector.

+\section{Secondary counting bounds}
+
+\begin{corollary}[Coarse and mean bounds]\label{cor:secondary-bounds}
+For $n\geq3$, put $k=\omega(n)$ and $L(n)=\log\#\mathcal M_n$. Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}
+ \#\mathcal M_n
+ \leq\sum_{r=0}^k\binom{\Omega(F_n)}r
+ \leq n^k,
+\end{equation}
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:crude-maximal-order}
+ \limsup_{n\to\infty}
+ \frac{L(n)\log\log n}{(\log n)^2}\leq1,
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2\,\log\varphi+o(1))\frac n{\log n},
+ \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
+\end{equation}
+Moreover, as $x\to\infty$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:mean-logarithmic-growth}
+ \left(\frac{\log2}{4}+o(1)\right)x(\log\log x)^2
+ \leq\sum_{3\leq n\leq x}L(n)
+ \leq(1+o(1))x\log x\,\log\log x.
+\end{equation}
+\end{corollary}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Unique factorization injects $\mathcal M_n$ into the subsets of the
+$\Omega(F_n)$ prime powers dividing $F_n$. Theorem~
+\ref{article-thm:witness-classification} bounds the subset size by $k$,
+giving the first inequality in \eqref{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}.
+Since $2^{\Omega(F_n)}\leq F_n<2^{n-1}$, we have
+$\Omega(F_n)\leq n-2$, and
+$\sum_{r=0}^k\binom Nr\leq(N+1)^k$ gives the second.
+
+The classical maximal order of $\omega(n)$
+\cite[Theorem~22.11]{HardyWright2008Introduction} applied to
+$L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$ proves
+\eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order}. Since $\mathcal M_n$ is an antichain in the
+divisor lattice of $F_n$, Wigert's theorem \cite{Wigert1907Divisors} gives
+\[
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2+o(1))\frac{\log F_n}{\log\log F_n}.
+\]
+Binet's formula yields \eqref{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}.
+
+For the mean upper bound, use
+\cite{HardyRamanujan1917NormalPrimeFactors} in the form
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+O(x)
+\]
+and $L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$. For the lower bound, Tur\'an's second-moment
+form of the Hardy--Ramanujan theorem \cite{Turan1934HardyRamanujan} gives
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)^2=(1+o(1))x(\log\log x)^2.
+\]
+The lower half of \eqref{article-eq:private-cover-entropy-order}, after
+enlarging its absolute constant for $\omega(n)<3$, completes the proof.
+\end{proof}
+
+For a labelled $k$-set $V$, let $C_k$ be the number of irredundant covers of
+$V$ by nonempty subsets.
+
+\begin{proposition}[Sharp cumulative-data bound]
+\label{prop:sharp-cumulative-data-obstruction}
+Assign a real weight $w_S\geq1$ to every nonempty $S\subseteq V$, and put
+\[
+ Z_V(w)=\sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
+              \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}w_S,
+ \qquad A=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}w_S.
+\]
+Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}
+ Z_V(w)\geq C_k+A-(2^k-1).
+\end{equation}
+This is best possible for every $A\geq2^k-1$: equality is attained by
+\[
+ w_V=A-(2^k-2),\qquad w_S=1\quad(S\ne V).
+\]
+If $k\geq3$, this is the only equality profile.
+
+Consequently, if $n\geq3$ is odd and squarefree and $k=\omega(n)$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-rank-pure-bound}
+ \#\{m\in\mathcal M_n:\mu^2(m)=1\}
+ \geq C_k+\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1),
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-weighted-excess}
+ \mathcal W(n)\geq
+ 1+\frac{\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1)}{C_k}.
+\end{equation}
+Among positive weight profiles with the same total
+$\sum_{d\mid n,\ d>1}a(d)=\omega(F_n)$, this conclusion is exact. The
+extremizing profile is not asserted to occur among Fibonacci exact-rank
+multiplicities.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Write $w_S=1+x_S$ with $x_S\geq0$. For every minimal cover $\mathcal C$,
+\[
+ \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}(1+x_S)
+ \geq1+\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}x_S.
+\]
+Every nonempty $S\subseteq V$ occurs in a minimal cover: use $\{V\}$ for
+$S=V$, and otherwise use
+$\{S\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V\setminus S\}$. Summation proves
+\eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}. The only minimal cover containing
+$V$ is $\{V\}$, so the displayed profile attains equality.
+
+If $k\geq3$, every proper nonempty $S$ occurs in at least two minimal covers.
+For $|S|=1$, use the singleton partition and $\{S,V\setminus S\}$; for
+$|S|\geq2$, choose $s\in S$, $t\notin S$, and also use the cover consisting
+of $S$, $\{s,t\}$, and the remaining singletons. Equality therefore forces
+$x_S=0$ for every proper $S$.
+
+For odd squarefree $n$, nonempty subsets of $\mathcal P(n)$ correspond to
+divisors $d>1$ of $n$, and exact ranks partition the prime divisors of $F_n$:
+\[
+ \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}a(n_S)=\omega(F_n).
+\]
+Apply \eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}, Theorem~
+\ref{article-cor:canonical-squarefree-slice}, and
+\eqref{article-eq:weighted-cover-excess}.
+\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
-For every $n\ge2$,
-\[
-B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.

-By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}, an integer $q$ lies in $D_m$ if and
-only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$. Thus $q\in D_n$ lies outside
-$\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}$ precisely when $\alpha(q)\mid n$ but

-If $\alpha(q)=n$, then clearly $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every $p\mid n$, so
-$q$ is outside the union. Conversely, suppose $\alpha(q)\mid n$ and
-$\alpha(q)<n$. Then $n/\alpha(q)>1$; choose a prime $p$ dividing
-$n/\alpha(q)$. Since $\alpha(q)\mid n/p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}

-$\alpha(r)\mid n$. Since $q\mid r$, every Fibonacci number divisible by $r$

-$F_{\alpha(r)}$ gives $\alpha(q)\mid\alpha(r)$. But $\alpha(q)=n$, so
-$n\mid\alpha(r)$ and $\alpha(r)\mid n$, whence $\alpha(r)=n$. Therefore
-$r\in B_n$.

+Let $D_n=\operatorname{Div}(F_n)$. The exact rank fiber can be read directly
+inside this divisor lattice.

+\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
+For every $n\geq2$,
+\[
+ B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.

-\subsection*{Witness covers}
-
-\begin{definition}\label{def:witness-cover}
-An \emph{$n$-witness cover} is a finite set
-$\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ of rank-jump prime powers satisfying:
-\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
-\item $d(\theta)\mid n$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$;
-\item the elements of $\Theta$ are pairwise coprime;
-\item the full-coordinate supports cover all prime coordinates of $n$,
-\[
-\bigcup_{\theta\in\Theta}T_n(\theta)=\mathcal P(n);
-\]
-\item each rank-jump factor has an essential coordinate not supplied by the other rank-jump factors,
-\[
-E_n(\theta)\nsubseteq
-\bigcup_{\eta\in\Theta,\ \eta\ne\theta}T_n(\eta)
-\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).
-\]
-\end{enumerate}
-The last condition is the irredundance condition. It is stated with
-$E_n$ rather than $T_n$ because overlapping full-coordinate support is
-allowed; what is forbidden is that every coordinate lost by lowering
-$\theta$ is already supplied at full exponent by the remaining rank-jump factors.
-\end{definition}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Coordinate test for lowering one rank-jump factor]
-\label{lem:coordinate-lowering-test}
-Let $n\ge2$, and let
-$\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$ be a pairwise coprime set of rank-jump
-prime powers with $d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and
-\[
-\lcmop(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r))=n.
-\]
-Fix $\theta_i=p_i^{e_i}$, and put
-\[
-N_i^-:=\lcmop\bigl(d^-(\theta_i),\ d(\theta_j):j\ne i\bigr).
-\]
-Then $N_i^-=n$ if and only if
-\[
-E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j).
-\]
-Equivalently, lowering $\theta_i$ to $p_i^{e_i-1}$ keeps the apparition lcm
-equal to $n$ exactly when every coordinate lost by the lowering is supplied at
-full exponent by some other rank-jump factor. If
-$\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, then
-$\nu_\ell(N_i^-)<\nu_\ell(n)$, so $N_i^-<n$.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Since $d^-(\theta_i)\mid d(\theta_i)\mid n$ and $d(\theta_j)\mid n$ for
-$j\ne i$, the integer $N_i^-$ divides $n$. Hence $N_i^-=n$ is equivalent to
-saying that every prime coordinate $\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$ occurs in $N_i^-$
-with valuation $\nu_\ell(n)$.
-
-Assume first that
-$E_n(\theta_i)\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$, and fix
-$\ell\in\mathcal P(n)$. Because the original lcm is $n$, at least one of the
-numbers $d(\theta_1),\ldots,d(\theta_r)$ supplies the full
-$\ell$-adic valuation of $n$. If such a supplier is some $d(\theta_j)$ with
-$j\ne i$, then $\ell\in T_n(\theta_j)$ and the same full valuation appears in
-$N_i^-$. The only remaining case is that $\theta_i$ itself supplies the full
-valuation and no other rank-jump factor does, so $\ell\in T_n(\theta_i)$ and
-$\ell\notin\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The assumed containment then gives
-$\ell\notin E_n(\theta_i)$. By the definition of $E_n(\theta_i)$,
-$\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))=\nu_\ell(n)$, so the lowered factor still supplies the
-full $\ell$-coordinate in $N_i^-$. Thus every coordinate of $n$ is still
-present at full valuation, and $N_i^-=n$.
-
-Conversely, suppose that some coordinate
-$\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ is not in $\bigcup_{j\ne i}T_n(\theta_j)$. The
-membership $\ell\in E_n(\theta_i)$ says
-$\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta_i))<\nu_\ell(n)$. For every $j\ne i$, the exclusion
-$\ell\notin T_n(\theta_j)$ says
-$\nu_\ell(d(\theta_j))<\nu_\ell(n)$. Therefore the lcm defining $N_i^-$ also
-has $\ell$-adic valuation strictly below $\nu_\ell(n)$. Since $N_i^-\mid n$,
-this proves $N_i^-<n$.
+\begin{lemma}[Minimal-lcm criterion]\label{thm:minimal-generators}
+Let $n\geq2$, and let $m=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ divide $F_n$, with the
+$p_i$ distinct. Put
+\[
+ \lambda_i=\alpha(p_i^{e_i}),\qquad
+ \lambda_i^-=\alpha(p_i^{e_i-1}).
+\]
+Then $m\in\mathcal M_n$ if and only if
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm-criterion}
+ \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)=n
+\end{equation}
+and, for every $i$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:lowered-lcm-criterion}
+ \lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,
+        \lambda_{i+1},\ldots,\lambda_r)<n.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Repeated use of Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives
+$\alpha(m)=\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)$ and replaces $\lambda_i$ by
+$\lambda_i^-$ for $m/p_i$. Thus minimality implies both displays. Conversely,
+if they hold and $q$ is a proper divisor of $m$, then for some $i$ the
+$p_i$-exponent of $q$ is at most $e_i-1$, so
+\[
+ \alpha(q)\mid\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_i^-,\ldots,\lambda_r)<n.
+\]
+Hence no proper divisor of $m$ belongs to $B_n$.
 \end{proof}
 
-\begin{proposition}[Wagner comparison and lowered labels]
-\label{prop:wagner-comparison}
-Let $n\ge2$, and let $\Theta=\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$ be a set of distinct prime
-rank-jump factors with $d_i:=\alpha(p_i)\mid n$. Then $\Theta$ is an $n$-witness cover
-if and only if, after forgetting the order of the tuple
-$(d_1,\ldots,d_r)$,
+\begin{proposition}[Wagner comparison]\label{prop:wagner-comparison}
+Let $\Theta=\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$ be distinct prime jumps with
+$d_i=\alpha(p_i)\mid n$. Then $\Theta$ is an $n$-witness cover if and only if
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover}
  \lcmop(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=n,
  \qquad
  \lcmop(d_1,\ldots,\widehat{d_i},\ldots,d_r)<n
- \quad(1\le i\le r).
+ \quad(1\leq i\leq r).
 \end{equation}
-Thus the prime-jump case is precisely the unordered form of Wagner's minimal
-multiplicative cover condition.
-
-For arbitrary pairwise coprime jumps
-$\Theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\}$, the witness condition replaces the
-deletion in \eqref{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover} by
+For arbitrary pairwise coprime rank jumps, the second condition becomes
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:lowered-label-multiplicative-cover}
- \lcmop\bigl(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d^-(\theta_i),\ldots,
- d(\theta_r)\bigr)<n
- \quad(1\le i\le r).
+ \lcmop(d(\theta_1),\ldots,d^-(\theta_i),\ldots,d(\theta_r))<n
+ \quad(1\leq i\leq r).
 \end{equation}
-In particular, ladder jumps supply the predecessor-decorated case: their
-label is lowered to $d^-(\theta_i)$ rather than deleted.
 \end{proposition}
 
 \begin{proof}
-For a prime jump $p_i$, one has $d^-(p_i)=\alpha(1)=1$. Hence replacing
-$d_i$ by $d^-(p_i)$ in an lcm is identical to omitting $d_i$. Lemma~
-\ref{thm:minimal-generators} and Lemma~\ref{lem:coordinate-lowering-test}
-then identify the witness-cover conditions with
-\eqref{eq:wagner-minimal-multiplicative-cover}. Since the labels form a
-minimal cover, no repeated label can occur; forgetting tuple order therefore
-produces the corresponding unordered cover without a multiplicity ambiguity.
-
-For arbitrary rank-jump factors, the same two lemmas say exactly that the full apparition
-lcm is $n$ and that lowering each rank-jump factor produces
-\eqref{eq:lowered-label-multiplicative-cover}. The final assertion is the
-distinction between $d^-(p)=1$ for prime jumps and the nontrivial lower rank
-of a ladder jump.
+For a prime jump $p_i$, $d^-(p_i)=\alpha(1)=1$, so lowering its label is the
+same as deleting it. In general, the full supports cover $\mathcal P(n)$
+exactly when the lcm of the labels is $n$. After $\theta_i$ is lowered, that

+arithmetic multiplicity is the only term beyond the support combinatorics in
+our principal bound.
 
-For a general $n$, let $R(n)$ be the largest number of rank-jump prime powers
-having one fixed essential/full support pair.  Private-coordinate encoding and
-the rank-pure construction give, for $k=\omega(n)\ge3$,
-\[
- (2^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}-1)^{\lceil k/2\rceil}
- \le\#\mathcal M_n
- \le\sum_{s=1}^k\binom{k}{s}(2R(n))^s2^{s(k-s)}.
-\]
-Hence
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-entropy-bounds}

+\begin{theorem}[Support bound]
+\label{thm:minimal-generator-growth}
+Let $n\geq3$, $k=\omega(n)$, and $L(n)=\log\#\mathcal M_n$. Then
+$\mathcal M_n$ is nonempty. If $k\geq3$ and $r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}
+ (2^r-1)^{k-r}
+ \leq\#\mathcal M_n
+ \leq\sum_{s=1}^k\binom{k}{s}(2R(n))^s2^{s(k-s)}.
+\end{equation}
+Uniformly when $\omega(n)\to\infty$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}

+ \leq L(n)
+ \leq\frac{\log2}{4}\omega(n)^2+
+       \omega(n)\log R(n)+O(\omega(n)).
 \end{equation}
-The lower estimate already gives the target constant after the
-Hardy--Ramanujan normal-order theorem.  The upper estimate proves

-above is necessary; it is not sufficient because the complementary ladder and

- \left(\frac{\log\varphi}{2}+o(1)\right)

-\]
-These are Theorems~\ref{thm:mean-rank-window-deaggregation} and

-bound $\log\mathcal W(n)$ at the scale required above, and the cumulative

-Proposition~\ref{prop:sharp-cumulative-data-obstruction} makes one limitation

-\subsection*{Organization}
+Wagner's minimal multiplicative covers
+\cite{Wagner1978MultiplicativeCovers} supply the classical prime-jump
+skeleton: deleting one lcm label must lower the lcm. Fibonacci prime-power
+lifting adds the predecessor $d^-(\theta)$, so a ladder label must be lowered
+rather than deleted. Theorem~\ref{thm:witness-classification} identifies
+exactly which such covers are the minimal rank fibers.
 
-Section~\ref{sec:prelim} records the classical rank and primitive-divisor
-inputs. Section~\ref{sec:upper-fibers} gives the Wagner comparison and proves
-the witness-cover classification. Section~\ref{sec:prime-power-realization}
-proves the prime-power lifting, prime--ladder dichotomy, and unique ladder-slot
-formula. Section~\ref{sec:rank-pure} develops the canonical squarefree slice,
-its weighted count, the labelled cover asymptotic, and worked examples.
-Section~\ref{sec:growth} proves the rank-window, fibotomic, support-entropy,
-and large-primitive-divisor bounds. Section~\ref{sec:inverse-dynamics} gives the short inverse-ray
-application, and the final section states the remaining arithmetic
-interfaces. The submitted supplement contains the connected-block
-factorization, exact support spectra, complete classifications for
-$\omega(n)\le4$, secondary asymptotics, and finite checks, all with numbered
-cross-references.
+The arithmetic realization uses the classical existence of an exact-rank
+prime for every rank $n\geq3$ except $6$ and $12$, following Carmichael and
+Bilu--Hanrot--Voutier
+\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}.
+The multiplicities $a(d)$ retain information not supplied by existence alone;

-\begin{proposition}[Finite divisor/rank verification with supplied factorization]
-\label{prop:effective-birth-layer-computation}
-Let $n\ge2$ and suppose the integer factorization of $F_n$ is known. Then
-$B_n$, $A(n)$, and $\mathcal M_n$ are recovered exactly by the following finite
-divisor/rank test.
-\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
-\item Enumerate the divisor set $D_n=\operatorname{Div}(F_n)$ from the
- factorization of $F_n$.
-\item Enumerate the divisor set $\operatorname{Div}(n)$. For each
- $q\in D_n$, compute
- \[
- \alpha_n(q):=\min\{d\mid n:q\mid F_d\}.
- \]
-\item Set $B_n=\{q\in D_n:q\ge2,\ \alpha_n(q)=n\}$ and
- $A(n)=\#B_n$.
-\item Sort $B_n$ by divisibility-compatible order, for instance by size, and
- retain exactly those $m\in B_n$ for which no previously retained element
- divides $m$; the retained set is $\mathcal M_n$.
-\end{enumerate}
-\end{proposition}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Since every $q\in D_n$ divides $F_n$, Proposition~\ref{article-prop:rank-basics}
-shows that $q\mid F_d$ for some $d$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid d$. In
-particular $q\mid F_n$ implies $\alpha(q)\mid n$, so the least positive index
-at which $q$ appears is exactly
-\[
-\alpha(q)=\min\{d\mid n:q\mid F_d\}=\alpha_n(q).
-\]
-Hence the test in step (c) gives precisely the definition
-$B_n=\{q\in D_n:\alpha(q)=n\}$, with the harmless exclusion of $q=1$ already
-consistent with the convention $\alpha(1)=1$ and $n\ge2$. Counting this set
-gives $A(n)$.
-
-It remains to justify step (d). The set $B_n$ is finite. If its elements are
-processed in increasing size, then every proper divisor of the current element
-has already been processed. We claim inductively that every discarded element
-has a retained minimal divisor. The claim is vacuous before the first element.
-If the current element is discarded, it has a previously retained divisor by
-the algorithm, so the claim holds for it; if it is retained, it is its own
-retained divisor. Thus every earlier divisor, retained or discarded, has a
-retained divisor below it. Consequently the current element is retained if and
-only if no smaller element of $B_n$ divides it, which is exactly minimality in
-the divisibility poset. The retained set is therefore $\mathcal M_n$.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{remark}[Reproducibility scope]
-The preceding proposition is used only to document the finite verification
-interface for the table, not as a complexity theorem.  After the factorization
-of $F_n$ has been supplied, the displayed loops involve only the finite divisor
-sets of $F_n$ and $n$, ordinary divisibility tests $q\mid F_d$, and divisor
-comparisons inside $B_n$.  The manuscript makes no bit-complexity assertion and
-does not include the cost of factoring $F_n$ in the numerical evidence.
-\end{remark}

-\subsection{Rank of apparition and Fibonacci divisibility}\label{subsec:fib-div}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Finite rank of apparition]\label{lem:finite-rank}
-For every integer $q\ge1$, the rank of apparition $\alpha(q)$ is finite.  More
-precisely, $\alpha(1)=1$, and for every $q\ge2$ there is a positive integer
-$r$ such that $q\mid F_r$.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The case $q=1$ is the stated convention.  Let $q\ge2$.  Work modulo $q$ with
-the Fibonacci state vector $(F_m,F_{m+1})$.  The transition
-\[
-(x,y)\longmapsto (y,x+y)
-\]
-has inverse $(x,y)\mapsto (y-x,x)$ modulo $q$, so it is a permutation of the
-finite set $(\ZZ/q\ZZ)^2$.  Therefore the orbit of the initial state $(0,1)$
-is periodic and returns to $(0,1)$ after some positive number $r$ of steps.
-Thus $(F_r,F_{r+1})\equiv(0,1)\pmod q$, in particular $q\mid F_r$.  The
-least such positive $r$ exists by well ordering.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{proposition}\label{prop:rank-basics}
-Let $q,u,v\ge1$ and let $a,b,m\ge1$. Then:
-\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
-\item $q\mid F_m$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$.
-\item $\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$.
-\item $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))=\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$.
-\end{enumerate}
-\end{proposition}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The divisibility criterion and the strong-divisibility identity are classical;
-we use them in the forms proved by Wall \cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm} and
-Vinson \cite{Vinson1963RankApparition}. The convention $\alpha(1)=1$ makes
-the assertion for $q=1$ immediate.
+\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:prelim}
 
-The Fibonacci lcm identity is recorded by Luca--Tron
-\cite{LucaTron2015SelfFibonacciDivisors}; Renault gives the corresponding
-identity for the more general $(a,b)$-Fibonacci sequences
-\cite{Renault2013PeriodRankOrder}. For completeness, an integer $m$ is
-divisible by
-$\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ if and only if $\lcmop(u,v)\mid F_m$, by (i). This is
-equivalent to $u\mid F_m$ and $v\mid F_m$, hence to
-$\alpha(u)\mid m$ and $\alpha(v)\mid m$, again by (i). Thus the multiples of
-$\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ are exactly the multiples of
-$\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$, and the two positive integers are equal.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Exact-rank primes and primitive divisors}\label{subsec:primitive}
-
-A prime $p$ is an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} if $\alpha(p)=d$;
-when it is viewed as a rank-jump prime power, we also call it a \emph{prime
-jump}. We reserve \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} for the standard
-Carmichael--Bilu--Hanrot--Voutier convention: a prime $p$ dividing $F_d$ is
-primitive when
-\[
- p\nmid 5F_1F_2\cdots F_{d-1}.
-\]
-Thus every primitive divisor is an exact-rank prime, but the exact-rank prime
-$5$ at rank $5$ is excluded from the primitive-divisor terminology because it
-divides the discriminant. This distinction will be maintained throughout.
-
-\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
-For every $n\ge 3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there exists a prime $p_n$ with
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For $n=3,4,5$ one takes $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$; the last is the
-discriminant-related exact-rank exception just described. For $n\ge 7$,
-$n\neq 12$, the primitive divisor theorem
-\cite{Carmichael1913PrimitiveDivisors,Yabuta2001PrimitiveDivisorFibonacci,%
-BiluHanrotVoutier2001PrimitiveDivisorsLucas}
-gives a prime dividing $F_n$ but no earlier Fibonacci number. Since
-$\alpha(p_n)\mid n$ and $p_n$ divides no $F_d$ with $d<n$, necessarily
-$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Counting corollaries}\label{subsec:counting}
-
-The standard M\"obius-inversion formulas for first-appearance counts follow
-from Stroi\'nski's $\alpha$-contraction identity
-\cite{Stroinski2016AlphaContraction}: for any $f:\NN\to\mathbb{C}$ with
-$f(1)=0$,
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stroinski}
-\sum_{d\mid F_n}f(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}f_\alpha(d),
-\qquad
-f_\alpha(d):=\sum_{\alpha(m)=d}f(m).
-\end{equation}
-Taking $f$ to be the indicator of integers at least $2$, of primes, or of
-prime powers, and applying M\"obius inversion, one obtains
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:mobius-birth}
-A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\tau(F_d),
-\qquad
-A_{\mathrm{pr}}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)\,\omega(F_d).
-\end{equation}
-We regard these as known corollaries; the witness-cover classification below
-is independent of them.
-
-\begin{lemma}[Exact-rank prime M\"obius count]\label{lem:primitive-prime-mobius-count}
-For $d\ge1$, put
-\[
-\Pi_\alpha(d):=\{p\text{ prime}:\alpha(p)=d\}.
-\]
-Then $\Pi_\alpha(d)$ is finite and
-\[
-\#\Pi_\alpha(d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\mu(d/c)\,\omega(F_c).
-\]
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For each $d\ge1$, the primes with rank dividing $d$ are exactly the prime
-divisors of $F_d$: indeed, for a prime $p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}
-gives $p\mid F_d$ if and only if $\alpha(p)\mid d$.  Hence
-Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} partitions the distinct prime divisors of
-$F_d$ according to their exact ranks $c\mid d$, including the exceptional
-primes $2$ and $5$ with ranks $3$ and $5$ respectively; a prime divisor of
-$F_c$ can occur earlier only through the condition $\alpha(p)\mid e$ for the
-earlier index $e$.
-\[
-\omega(F_d)=\sum_{c\mid d}\#\Pi_\alpha(c).
-\]
-The right-hand side is finite because $F_d$ has only finitely many prime
-divisors.  Applying M\"obius inversion on the divisor lattice of $d$ gives the
-displayed formula.
-\end{proof}

-\subsection{Rank-jump notation}\label{subsec:prime-power}
-
-\begin{definition}\label{def:rank-jump-families}
-For a prime power $\theta=p^e$ with $e\ge1$, put
-\[
-d(\theta):=\alpha(\theta),\qquad
-d^-(\theta):=\alpha(p^{e-1}),
-\]
-where $\alpha(1)=1$. For $d\ge1$ define
-\[
-\Atom(d):=\{p^e:\ \alpha(p^e)=d,\ \alpha(p^{e-1})<d\}.
-\]
-Thus $\Atom(d)$ consists of the prime-power factors at which the rank first
-jumps to $d$ when the exponent is increased.
-
-If $d(\theta)\mid n$, define the full-coordinate support and the
-essential-coordinate support of $\theta$ relative to $n$ by
-\[
-T_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\
-\nu_\ell(d(\theta))=\nu_\ell(n)\},
-\]
-and
-\[
-E_n(\theta):=\{\ell\in T_n(\theta):\
-\nu_\ell(d^-(\theta))<\nu_\ell(n)\}.
-\]
-Equivalently, $T_n(\theta)$ records the prime coordinates of $n$ supplied at
-full exponent by $d(\theta)$, while $E_n(\theta)$ records the full coordinates
-lost when $\theta=p^e$ is lowered to $p^{e-1}$.
-
-For nonempty $I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, put
-\[
-\mathcal A_{I,J}(n):=
-\{\theta\in\bigcup_{d\mid n}\Atom(d):\
-E_n(\theta)=I,\ T_n(\theta)=J\}.
-\]
-\end{definition}
+The finiteness of $\alpha(q)$ follows from the periodicity of the Fibonacci
+state vector modulo $q$; see, for example, Wall
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm}. We use the following standard facts.
+
+\begin{proposition}\label{prop:rank-basics}
+For positive integers $q,u,v,a,b,m$,
+\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
+\item $q\mid F_m$ if and only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$;
+\item $\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$;
+\item $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))=\lcmop(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))$.
+\end{enumerate}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The first two statements are classical
+\cite{Wall1960FibonacciModm,Vinson1963RankApparition}. For the last, an integer
+$m$ is divisible by $\alpha(\lcmop(u,v))$ exactly when both $u$ and $v$
+divide $F_m$, hence exactly when both $\alpha(u)$ and $\alpha(v)$ divide $m$.
+The two sides therefore have the same positive multiples. This lcm identity
+also appears in \cite{LucaTron2015SelfFibonacciDivisors,Renault2013PeriodRankOrder}.
+\end{proof}
+
+We call $p$ an \emph{exact-rank prime of rank $d$} when $\alpha(p)=d$.
+The term \emph{primitive divisor of $F_d$} retains its standard meaning: a
+prime dividing $F_d$ but not $5F_1\cdots F_{d-1}$. Thus the exact-rank prime
+$5$ at rank $5$ is not primitive in this terminology.
+
+\begin{theorem}[Classical exact-rank existence]
+\label{thm:primitive-divisors}
+For every $n\geq3$ with $n\notin\{6,12\}$, there is a prime $p_n$ such that
+$\alpha(p_n)=n$.
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Take $p_3=2$, $p_4=3$, and $p_5=5$. For $n\geq7$, $n\ne12$, the primitive

+\section{Quantitative bounds}\label{sec:growth}
+
+For $n\geq3$, define the rank-window multiplicity precisely by
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-window-multiplicity}
+ R(n):=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}
+ \#\mathcal A_{I,J}(n)\right\}.
+\end{equation}
+Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-jump-family-ladder-slots} shows that this number is
+finite: prime-jump families are finite unions of exact-rank prime classes,
+and each ladder family contains at most one factor.
+
+\begin{lemma}[Deaggregation of a rank window]
+\label{lem:rank-window-deaggregation}
+For $d\mid n$, put
+\[
+ T_n(d)=\{\ell\in\mathcal P(n):\nu_\ell(d)=\nu_\ell(n)\}
+\]
+and
+\[
+ A^*(n)=\max\!\left\{1,
+ \max_{\substack{d\mid n\\T_n(d)\ne\varnothing}}a(d)\right\}.
+\]
+If $n=\prod_\ell\ell^{e_\ell}$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}
+ 0\leq\log R(n)-\log A^*(n)
+ \leq\log2+\sum_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}\log e_\ell.
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+For nonempty $J\subseteq\mathcal P(n)$, let
+\[
+ W_J(n)=\{d\mid n:T_n(d)=J\}.
+\]
+Then $\#W_J(n)=\prod_{\ell\notin J}e_\ell$, and the prime jumps with
+$(E_n,T_n)=(J,J)$ form the disjoint union of the classes
+$\Pi_\alpha(d)$ for $d\in W_J(n)$. All other nonempty families are ladder
+families of size at most one. Hence, with
+\[
+ P(n)=\max_{J\ne\varnothing}\sum_{d\in W_J(n)}a(d),
+\]
+we have $P(n)\leq R(n)\leq P(n)+1$. It follows that
+\[
+ A^*(n)\leq R(n)
+ \leq1+A^*(n)\prod_{\ell^{e_\ell}\parallel n}e_\ell,
+\]
+which gives \eqref{eq:pointwise-window-deaggregation}.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal-generator-growth}]
+For $n\geq3$, the strict increase of the Fibonacci sequence from index $2$
+onward gives $\alpha(F_n)=n$. Thus $B_n$ is a nonempty finite poset and
+$\mathcal M_n\ne\varnothing$.
+
+Assume $k\geq3$, order $\mathcal P(n)$, and put $r=\lfloor k/2\rfloor$.
+Choose an $r$-set
+$P\subseteq\mathcal P(n)\setminus\{2,3\}$ and put
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. For each map
+\[
+ H:Q\longrightarrow2^P\setminus\{\varnothing\}
+\]
+and $i\in P$, define
+\[
+ T_i=\{i\}\cup\{q\in Q:i\in H(q)\}.
+\]
+The integer $n_{T_i}$ has a prime divisor outside $\{2,3\}$, so it is not
+$6$ or $12$. Choose an exact-rank prime $\pi_{T_i}$ of rank $n_{T_i}$ by
+Theorem~\ref{thm:primitive-divisors}. The supports $T_i$ cover
+$\mathcal P(n)$, and $i$ is private to $T_i$; hence the primes $\pi_{T_i}$
+form a witness cover. Different maps give different support families and,
+by unique factorization, different elements of $\mathcal M_n$. There are
+$(2^r-1)^{k-r}$ such maps, proving the lower bound.
+
+For the upper bound, let $\Theta$ be a witness cover with $s$ factors. Choose
+the least private coordinate $x_\theta$ of each $\theta\in\Theta$. These
+coordinates are distinct; write $P=\{x_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ and
+$Q=\mathcal P(n)\setminus P$. If $x_\theta=x$, then
+\[
+ T_n(\theta)=\{x\}\cup U_\theta,\qquad U_\theta\subseteq Q.
+\]
+By Lemma~\ref{thm:primitive-ladder-dichotomy}, either
+$E_n(\theta)=T_n(\theta)$ or $E_n(\theta)=\{x\}$. For fixed $x$ this gives
+at most $2R(n)2^{k-s}$ choices. Ignoring coverage and coprimeness only
+increases the count, so summing over the $\binom{k}{s}$ possible private sets
+and $1\leq s\leq k$ proves the upper bound in
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-finite-bounds}.
+
+Finally, $r(k-r)=\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor$ and
+$(k-r)\log(1-2^{-r})=O(1)$. For the upper bound use
+$s(k-s)\leq k^2/4$, $s\leq k$, and
+$\sum_s\binom{k}{s}\leq2^k$. Taking logarithms gives
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order}.
+\end{proof}
+
+The term $\omega(n)\log R(n)$ depends on the multiplicities $a(d)$ of
+individual exact ranks, as Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-window-deaggregation} makes
+explicit. Presently available existence and cumulative primitive-divisor
+estimates do not remove this term. Consequently
+\eqref{eq:private-cover-entropy-order} does not give an unconditional
+almost-all equivalent for $\log\#\mathcal M_n$; such a result would also have
+to control witness covers outside the rank-pure sector.

+\section{Secondary counting bounds}
+
+\begin{corollary}[Coarse and mean bounds]\label{cor:secondary-bounds}
+For $n\geq3$, put $k=\omega(n)$ and $L(n)=\log\#\mathcal M_n$. Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}
+ \#\mathcal M_n
+ \leq\sum_{r=0}^k\binom{\Omega(F_n)}r
+ \leq n^k,
+\end{equation}
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:crude-maximal-order}
+ \limsup_{n\to\infty}
+ \frac{L(n)\log\log n}{(\log n)^2}\leq1,
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2\,\log\varphi+o(1))\frac n{\log n},
+ \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
+\end{equation}
+Moreover, as $x\to\infty$,
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:mean-logarithmic-growth}
+ \left(\frac{\log2}{4}+o(1)\right)x(\log\log x)^2
+ \leq\sum_{3\leq n\leq x}L(n)
+ \leq(1+o(1))x\log x\,\log\log x.
+\end{equation}
+\end{corollary}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Unique factorization injects $\mathcal M_n$ into the subsets of the
+$\Omega(F_n)$ prime powers dividing $F_n$. Theorem~
+\ref{article-thm:witness-classification} bounds the subset size by $k$,
+giving the first inequality in \eqref{eq:finite-minimal-generator-bound}.
+Since $2^{\Omega(F_n)}\leq F_n<2^{n-1}$, we have
+$\Omega(F_n)\leq n-2$, and
+$\sum_{r=0}^k\binom Nr\leq(N+1)^k$ gives the second.
+
+The classical maximal order of $\omega(n)$
+\cite[Theorem~22.11]{HardyWright2008Introduction} applied to
+$L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$ proves
+\eqref{eq:crude-maximal-order}. Since $\mathcal M_n$ is an antichain in the
+divisor lattice of $F_n$, Wigert's theorem \cite{Wigert1907Divisors} gives
+\[
+ L(n)\leq\log\tau(F_n)
+ \leq(\log2+o(1))\frac{\log F_n}{\log\log F_n}.
+\]
+Binet's formula yields \eqref{eq:sperner-wigert-envelope}.
+
+For the mean upper bound, use
+\cite{HardyRamanujan1917NormalPrimeFactors} in the form
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+O(x)
+\]
+and $L(n)\leq\omega(n)\log n$. For the lower bound, Tur\'an's second-moment
+form of the Hardy--Ramanujan theorem \cite{Turan1934HardyRamanujan} gives
+\[
+ \sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n)^2=(1+o(1))x(\log\log x)^2.
+\]
+The lower half of \eqref{article-eq:private-cover-entropy-order}, after
+enlarging its absolute constant for $\omega(n)<3$, completes the proof.
+\end{proof}
+
+For a labelled $k$-set $V$, let $C_k$ be the number of irredundant covers of
+$V$ by nonempty subsets.
+
+\begin{proposition}[Sharp cumulative-data bound]
+\label{prop:sharp-cumulative-data-obstruction}
+Assign a real weight $w_S\geq1$ to every nonempty $S\subseteq V$, and put
+\[
+ Z_V(w)=\sum_{\mathcal C\in\operatorname{MinCov}(V)}
+              \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}w_S,
+ \qquad A=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}w_S.
+\]
+Then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}
+ Z_V(w)\geq C_k+A-(2^k-1).
+\end{equation}
+This is best possible for every $A\geq2^k-1$: equality is attained by
+\[
+ w_V=A-(2^k-2),\qquad w_S=1\quad(S\ne V).
+\]
+If $k\geq3$, this is the only equality profile.
+
+Consequently, if $n\geq3$ is odd and squarefree and $k=\omega(n)$, then
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-rank-pure-bound}
+ \#\{m\in\mathcal M_n:\mu^2(m)=1\}
+ \geq C_k+\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1),
+\end{equation}
+and
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:squarefree-cumulative-weighted-excess}
+ \mathcal W(n)\geq
+ 1+\frac{\omega(F_n)-(2^k-1)}{C_k}.
+\end{equation}
+Among positive weight profiles with the same total
+$\sum_{d\mid n,\ d>1}a(d)=\omega(F_n)$, this conclusion is exact. The
+extremizing profile is not asserted to occur among Fibonacci exact-rank
+multiplicities.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Write $w_S=1+x_S$ with $x_S\geq0$. For every minimal cover $\mathcal C$,
+\[
+ \prod_{S\in\mathcal C}(1+x_S)
+ \geq1+\sum_{S\in\mathcal C}x_S.
+\]
+Every nonempty $S\subseteq V$ occurs in a minimal cover: use $\{V\}$ for
+$S=V$, and otherwise use
+$\{S\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V\setminus S\}$. Summation proves
+\eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}. The only minimal cover containing
+$V$ is $\{V\}$, so the displayed profile attains equality.
+
+If $k\geq3$, every proper nonempty $S$ occurs in at least two minimal covers.
+For $|S|=1$, use the singleton partition and $\{S,V\setminus S\}$; for
+$|S|\geq2$, choose $s\in S$, $t\notin S$, and also use the cover consisting
+of $S$, $\{s,t\}$, and the remaining singletons. Equality therefore forces
+$x_S=0$ for every proper $S$.
+
+For odd squarefree $n$, nonempty subsets of $\mathcal P(n)$ correspond to
+divisors $d>1$ of $n$, and exact ranks partition the prime divisors of $F_n$:
+\[
+ \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathcal P(n)}a(n_S)=\omega(F_n).
+\]
+Apply \eqref{eq:sharp-total-mass-cover-bound}, Theorem~
+\ref{article-cor:canonical-squarefree-slice}, and
+\eqref{article-eq:weighted-cover-excess}.
+\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
-For every $n\ge2$,
-\[
-B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.
-\]
-Moreover $B_n$ is an upper set in $D_n$: if $q\in B_n$, $r\in D_n$, and
-$q\mid r$, then $r\in B_n$. Consequently
-\[
-B_n=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M_n}\{q\in D_n:\ m\mid q\}.
-\]
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}, an integer $q$ lies in $D_m$ if and
-only if $\alpha(q)\mid m$. Thus $q\in D_n$ lies outside
-$\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}$ precisely when $\alpha(q)\mid n$ but
-$\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every prime $p\mid n$.
-
-If $\alpha(q)=n$, then clearly $\alpha(q)\nmid n/p$ for every $p\mid n$, so
-$q$ is outside the union. Conversely, suppose $\alpha(q)\mid n$ and
-$\alpha(q)<n$. Then $n/\alpha(q)>1$; choose a prime $p$ dividing
-$n/\alpha(q)$. Since $\alpha(q)\mid n/p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics}
-gives $q\in D_{n/p}$, contrary to being outside the union. Hence the
-complement is exactly the set of $q\in D_n$ with $\alpha(q)=n$, namely
-$B_n$. For $n=2$ this also gives
-$B_2=D_2\setminus D_1=\varnothing$ under the boundary convention in
-Definition~\ref{def:birth-layer}.
-
-Now let $q\in B_n$, $r\in D_n$, and $q\mid r$. Since $r\in D_n$,
-$\alpha(r)\mid n$. Since $q\mid r$, every Fibonacci number divisible by $r$
-is divisible by $q$; applying the divisibility criterion to
-$F_{\alpha(r)}$ gives $\alpha(q)\mid\alpha(r)$. But $\alpha(q)=n$, so
-$n\mid\alpha(r)$ and $\alpha(r)\mid n$, whence $\alpha(r)=n$. Therefore
-$r\in B_n$.
-
-Finally $D_n$ is finite, so every element $q\in B_n$ has at least one
-minimal element $m$ of $B_n$ below it in the divisibility order. The upper-set
-property gives the reverse containment: every element of $D_n$ divisible by
-some $m\in\mathcal M_n$ lies again in $B_n$. This proves the displayed
-decomposition.
-\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Minimal-lcm criterion]\label{thm:minimal-generators}
-Let $n\ge2$, and let
-$m=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ be a divisor of $F_n$, with the $p_i$ distinct

-\[

-\]

-\begin{equation}\label{eq:lcm-criterion}
-\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)=n
-\quad\text{and}\quad
-\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_i^-,

-\quad(1\le i\le r).
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Because $m\mid F_n$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-basics} gives

-\[
-\alpha(m)=\lcmop(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r).
-\]
-Thus the first condition in \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion} is equivalent to

-still a divisor of $F_n$. Minimality of $m$ in $B_n$ implies
-$m/p_i\notin B_n$. Since $\alpha(m/p_i)\mid n$, this is equivalent to
-$\alpha(m/p_i)<n$. A second application of the lcm identity gives

-Conversely, suppose \eqref{eq:lcm-criterion} holds. The first condition gives

-\[

-\]
-again by the lcm identity and by monotonicity under divisibility of prime
-powers. The right-hand side is $<n$ by
-\eqref{eq:lcm-criterion}. Since $q\mid m\mid F_n$, we also have
-$\alpha(q)\mid n$, and therefore $\alpha(q)<n$. Thus no proper divisor of
-$m$ lies in $B_n$, so $m$ is minimal in $B_n$.
+Let $D_n=\operatorname{Div}(F_n)$. The exact rank fiber can be read directly
+inside this divisor lattice.

+\begin{lemma}[Upper-fiber identity]\label{thm:upper-fiber}
+For every $n\geq2$,
+\[
+ B_n=D_n\setminus\bigcup_{p\mid n}D_{n/p}.
+\]
+Moreover, $B_n$ is an upper set in $D_n$, and hence
+\[
+ B_n=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M_n}\{q\in D_n:m\mid q\}.

+\end{lemma}
